phy_edx.3.0.summary: A **wave** is a way of transferring **energy** and **information** from one place to another **without transferring matter**. In a water wave or a sound wave the particles of water or air only **oscillate (vibrate) about a fixed position**; it is the wave, carrying energy, that travels. You must be able to describe the evidence for this, such as a cork or floating object bobbing up and down on ripples without moving along, and air particles vibrating back and forth as sound passes without the air itself flowing from the source to the listener.

core.p: A wave is a **disturbance** that travels from one place to another. As it passes, each part of the medium (water, air, a rope, a spring) is pushed out of position and then pulled back, so it **oscillates** about where it started. The pattern of disturbance moves on; the particles do not.
bullets: Waves are caused by something **vibrating**: a loudspeaker cone, a dipper in a ripple tank, a hand shaking a rope.
The material the wave travels through is called the **medium**.
Each particle passes the disturbance on to its neighbour, so the **energy** is handed along the line of particles.
After the wave has passed, each particle ends up back at its **original position**.
Waves that need a medium (sound, water waves, waves on springs and ropes, seismic waves) are **mechanical waves**.
**Electromagnetic waves** (light, radio, microwaves) also transfer energy and information but do not need a medium: they can travel through a vacuum.

callouts.p: Waves transfer energy and information without transferring matter.

core.p: A wave carries energy away from its source. When the wave reaches something, it can transfer energy to it, for example making it move, heating it up or making it vibrate.
bullets: **Water waves** carry energy that can move boats, erode cliffs and can be used to generate electricity.
**Sound waves** carry energy that makes your **eardrum vibrate**; very loud sounds can even shatter glass.
**Light and infrared** from the Sun carry energy to the Earth, warming it and powering plant photosynthesis and solar cells.
**Microwaves** transfer energy to water molecules in food, heating it.
**Seismic waves** from earthquakes carry energy through the Earth that can damage buildings far from the source.
A bigger **amplitude** means the wave carries more energy (for example a louder sound or a bigger water wave).

callouts.p: What arrives at the far end is energy carried by the wave, not the water or air particles from the source.

core.p: Because a wave can be changed (its pattern, timing or strength), it can carry a message. That is why almost all communication uses waves.
bullets: **Sound waves** carry speech and music from a speaker to your ear.
**Radio waves** and **microwaves** carry TV, radio, mobile phone and satellite signals.
**Light** and **infrared** in optical fibres carry internet data.
**Ultrasound** echoes give information used to build images, for example of a fetus.
**Seismic waves** detected at different places give information about the structure of the Earth's interior.
In each case the information travels with the wave, while the medium itself stays where it is.

core.p: This is the heart of the spec point. In a wave, the particles of the medium **oscillate about a fixed (equilibrium) position**. They move back and forth or up and down, but they do not travel along with the wave. Only the energy moves from source to receiver.
bullets: In a **transverse** wave (such as ripples on water) particles move **up and down**, at right angles to the direction the wave travels.
In a **longitudinal** wave (such as sound in air) particles move **back and forth**, parallel to the direction the wave travels.
In both cases each particle's average position does not change over time.
Compare with a **current** or **wind**: there the water or air itself flows from place to place, which is transfer of matter, not a wave.
A stadium Mexican wave is a good picture: the wave goes round the stadium, but every person stays in their own seat.

head: Moving thing
Does it travel from source to receiver?
rows: No, they oscillate about a fixed position

callouts.p: Never say the particles move along with the wave or carry the energy across. Say the particles oscillate about a fixed position and pass the energy on.

core.h: Evidence from water waves: the floating cork
core.p: Put a cork, a ball or a small toy duck on the surface of water and send ripples past it. The ripples travel across the water, but the cork simply **bobs up and down** in the same place. If the water itself were travelling with the wave, the cork would be carried along with it.
bullets: The cork moves **up and down** as each crest and trough passes underneath.
The cork **does not move along** in the direction the wave travels.
Therefore the **water** does not travel with the wave; only the wave (and its energy) moves across the surface.
The cork moves at right angles to the wave direction, showing the water surface wave behaves as a **transverse** wave.
Seagulls sitting on the sea and boats at anchor bob up and down in the same way as waves pass.
In real oceans, floating objects can drift slowly because of wind and currents; that drift is not caused by the wave carrying water forward.

callouts.p: Point 1: the cork bobs up and down. Point 2: it does not move along with the wave, so the water does not travel with the wave.

core.h: Evidence from water waves: the ripple tank
core.p: In a ripple tank, a vibrating **dipper** makes circular or straight ripples that spread out across the water. A small floating object such as a leaf or a piece of paper placed on the water bobs in place as the ripples pass it.
bullets: The ripples (wavefronts) clearly **spread out** from the dipper to the edges of the tank.
The water does **not pile up** at the edges of the tank, so water is not being carried outwards.
A floating object **oscillates** where it is but stays in the same place.
The energy from the vibrating dipper is carried outwards to the sides of the tank.
The same idea explains why dropping a stone in a pond sends rings outwards while the pond water stays in the pond.

core.p: Sound is a **longitudinal** wave made by vibrating objects. A loudspeaker cone moves back and forth, pushing and pulling on the air next to it. This creates regions where air particles are squashed together (**compressions**) and spread apart (**rarefactions**), and this pattern travels outwards.
bullets: Each **air particle vibrates back and forth** about a fixed position, parallel to the direction the sound travels.
The air itself does **not flow** from the loudspeaker to the listener: if it did, you would feel a continuous wind blowing from every loudspeaker.
A **candle flame** placed in front of a loudspeaker playing a low note **flickers back and forth** but is not blown steadily away, showing the air oscillates rather than flowing.
Small polystyrene balls or rice grains on a drum skin jump up and down but are not thrown towards the listener.
When the sound reaches your ear, the vibrating air makes the **eardrum vibrate**, so energy and information have arrived even though the air near the speaker has not.
Sound needs a medium: a bell ringing inside a jar fades to silence as the air is pumped out, because there are no particles left to pass on the vibrations.

callouts.t: Sound is a vibration of particles
callouts.p: Sound travels as vibrations passed from particle to particle, so it cannot travel through a vacuum.

core.p: A slinky spring is a great model because you can watch one part of it while a wave passes. Tie a small piece of coloured **tape or ribbon** to one coil, then send waves along the spring.
bullets: **Longitudinal wave:** push and pull one end along the spring's length. Compressions and rarefactions travel along, but the tape moves **back and forth** about the same point.
**Transverse wave:** waggle one end from side to side. Humps travel along, but the tape moves **side to side** about the same point.
In both cases the tape ends up where it started once the wave has passed.
The energy from your hand travels to the far end of the spring, which may make an object there move.
The slinky models sound (longitudinal) and water ripples (transverse) and shows the same rule: the wave travels, the medium does not.

fig.cap: A longitudinal wave on a slinky. Compressions and rarefactions travel to the right, carrying energy, while the red tape on one coil only vibrates back and forth about its starting position.

core.p: All waves transfer energy and information without transferring matter, but they differ in whether they need a medium. This is useful context for explaining evidence.
bullets: **Mechanical waves** (sound, water waves, seismic waves, waves on ropes and springs) need particles to pass on the vibration.
Sound cannot travel through **space**, because space is a vacuum with no particles.
**Electromagnetic waves** are oscillating electric and magnetic fields; they need no medium and all travel at the same speed in a vacuum.
Light from the Sun crosses the vacuum of space, carrying energy and information to Earth, with no matter carried from the Sun to us by the wave.
For EM waves the idea of no matter being transferred is even clearer: there is no medium at all.

core.h: How to write about the evidence in an exam
core.p: Edexcel questions often describe an experiment (a cork, a duck, a candle, a slinky) and ask what it shows. Use a three-step structure: what you would see, what that means, and the conclusion.
bullets: **Observe:** the object moves up and down (water) or back and forth (sound, slinky).
**Notice:** it stays in the same place overall; it is not carried along with the wave.
**Conclude:** so the medium (water or air) does not travel with the wave; only the wave, and the energy it carries, travels.
Name the direction of oscillation correctly: up and down (transverse) for water waves, back and forth along the direction of travel (longitudinal) for sound.
Use the word **oscillate** or **vibrate about a fixed position**: these are the phrases mark schemes reward.

callouts.p: Many students describe the cork moving up and down but forget the conclusion. Always finish with: so the water does not move along with the wave.

core.p: Understanding that waves carry energy but not matter explains a huge range of everyday technology and natural events.
bullets: Communication systems can send messages across the world without moving any material from sender to receiver.
Sound from an orchestra fills a hall without any wind blowing across the audience.
Earthquake energy can cause damage hundreds of kilometres away even though rock from the epicentre stays put.
Wave power machines extract energy from waves at sea while the water stays roughly where it is.
Doctors use ultrasound waves to gain information about the inside of the body without cutting it open.

analogy.t: The Mexican wave in a stadium
analogy.p: In a Mexican wave each fan stands up and sits down in their own seat, but the wave races round the whole stadium. The fans are the particles of the medium; standing and sitting is their oscillation about a fixed position; the travelling pattern is the wave; and the excitement passed from fan to fan is like the energy. Nobody ends up in a different seat, just as no water or air is carried along by a wave. Where it breaks down: fans choose when to stand by watching their neighbours, whereas particles are pushed and pulled by forces from their neighbours; and fans move up and down only, so it models a transverse wave, not a longitudinal sound wave.

terms.d: A disturbance that transfers energy and information from one place to another without transferring matter.
The substance (such as water, air or a solid) through which a mechanical wave travels.
A repeated back and forth or up and down movement about a fixed (equilibrium) position.
The undisturbed position a particle returns to and oscillates about as a wave passes.
The movement of energy from one place or store to another; waves transfer energy from a source to a receiver.
A message or signal, such as sound, pictures or data, carried by a wave.
A wave that needs a medium to travel through, such as sound, water waves and seismic waves.
A transverse wave of oscillating electric and magnetic fields that can travel through a vacuum.
A wave in which the oscillations are perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer, such as ripples on water.
A wave in which the oscillations are parallel to the direction of energy transfer, such as sound.
A region in a longitudinal wave where particles are closer together than normal.
A region in a longitudinal wave where particles are further apart than normal.
A shallow tray of water in which a vibrating dipper makes water waves that can be observed.
A space containing no particles; sound cannot travel through it but electromagnetic waves can.

mistakes.w: The water moves along with the wave.
mistakes.r: The water particles oscillate up and down about a fixed position; only the wave and its energy travel.

mistakes.w: The cork moves up and down. (and nothing more)
mistakes.r: The cork moves up and down but does not move along with the wave, so the water is not transferred, only energy.

mistakes.w: Sound is air travelling from the speaker to your ear.
mistakes.r: Air particles vibrate back and forth about fixed positions, passing energy on; the air does not flow from the speaker to the listener.

mistakes.w: Waves transfer particles or matter.
mistakes.r: Waves transfer energy and information without transferring matter.

mistakes.w: In sound waves the particles move up and down.
mistakes.r: In sound (longitudinal) particles vibrate back and forth parallel to the direction the wave travels.

mistakes.w: The cork moves because the wave pushes it forward.
mistakes.r: The cork rises and falls as crests and troughs pass beneath it; there is no overall forward movement.

mistakes.w: Sound can travel through space.
mistakes.r: Sound needs a medium of particles; space is a vacuum, so sound cannot travel through it.

mistakes.w: Light waves need air to travel.
mistakes.r: Light is an electromagnetic wave and can travel through a vacuum.

exam.q: Complete the sentence: Waves transfer energy and information without transferring ______.
model: matter
exam.tip: Learn the key statement word for word.

exam.q: State two things that are transferred by a wave.
model: Energy
Information
exam.tip: Do not write particles or matter.

exam.q: A student puts a cork on the surface of water in a tank and makes waves travel across the water. Describe the motion of the cork.
model: The cork moves up and down
The cork stays in the same place / does not move along with the wave
exam.tip: Give both the direction of motion and the fact it is not carried along.

exam.q: Explain how the motion of the cork shows that a water wave does not transfer water.
model: The cork (and the water it floats on) only moves up and down about a fixed position
It does not travel in the direction of the wave, so the water is not carried along; only energy is transferred
exam.tip: Finish with a conclusion about the water, not just the cork.

exam.q: Describe how air particles move as a sound wave passes through the air.
model: Particles vibrate / oscillate back and forth
Parallel to the direction the wave travels, about a fixed position
exam.tip: Back and forth, not up and down.

exam.q: A candle flame is placed in front of a loudspeaker that is playing a low frequency note. The flame flickers back and forth. Explain what this shows about sound waves.
model: The air particles are vibrating back and forth / oscillating
The flame is not blown away from the speaker, so the air is not flowing / no air is transferred from the speaker
exam.tip: Link the observation to the idea that the air does not travel.

exam.q: Give one example of a wave transferring energy and one example of a wave transferring information.
model: Energy: e.g. Sun warming the Earth / microwaves heating food / sound making the eardrum vibrate / sea waves eroding cliffs
Information: e.g. radio or TV signals / mobile phone signals / speech / optical fibre data
exam.tip: Any correct specific example scores; be precise.

exam.q: Explain why sound cannot travel through space but light can.
model: Sound needs particles (a medium) to vibrate and pass on the energy; space is a vacuum
Light is an electromagnetic wave which does not need a medium
exam.tip: Mention vacuum and medium.

exam.q: A coloured piece of tape is attached to one coil of a slinky spring. A longitudinal wave is sent along the spring. Describe what happens to the tape and what this shows.
model: The tape moves back and forth along the length of the spring about the same position
Shows that the coils (medium) do not travel along with the wave; only energy is transferred
exam.tip: For longitudinal, the movement is along the spring, not side to side.

exam.q: Describe experiments using water waves and sound waves that provide evidence that it is the wave, and not the water or air itself, that travels.
model: Water: place a floating object such as a cork in a ripple tank or on a pond and make waves
The cork bobs up and down but does not move along with the waves
So the water is not carried along; only the wave travels
Sound: place a candle flame (or light paper or polystyrene balls) in front of a loudspeaker
The flame moves back and forth but is not blown away from the speaker
So air particles vibrate about fixed positions and the air does not flow from source to listener
Both show waves transfer energy (and information) without transferring matter
exam.tip: Level-marked: describe BOTH experiments, give observations and draw a conclusion for each.

worked.q: A rubber duck floats on a pond. A child throws in a stone and ripples spread out past the duck. Describe and explain what happens to the duck. (model answer)
steps: As a crest reaches the duck, the duck rises; as a trough passes, the duck falls.
The duck repeats this up and down motion as each ripple passes.
After the ripples have passed, the duck is in the same place it started.
This is because the water particles under the duck only oscillate up and down about a fixed position.
The ripples carry energy outwards from where the stone landed, but the water itself is not carried outwards.
worked.ans: The duck bobs up and down but stays in the same place, showing the wave transfers energy but not the water.

worked.q: Explain how a person standing 50 m away hears a drum, even though the air next to the drum does not reach them. (model answer)
steps: The drum skin vibrates, pushing and pulling the air particles next to it.
These particles collide with and push their neighbours, creating compressions and rarefactions.
Each particle vibrates back and forth about a fixed position, passing energy on to the next particle.
The pattern of compressions and rarefactions travels through the air to the listener.
The vibrating air makes the listener's eardrum vibrate, so energy and information arrive without any air travelling 50 m.
worked.ans: Energy is passed from particle to particle as a longitudinal wave; the air only vibrates in place, so the sound, not the air, travels.

phy_edx.3.1.summary: To describe any wave you need a precise vocabulary: **frequency**, **wavelength**, **amplitude**, **period**, **wave velocity** and **wavefront**, and you must be able to read each one off a wave diagram or graph. Waves come in two types: in **transverse** waves the oscillations are **perpendicular** to the direction of energy transfer, and in **longitudinal** waves they are **parallel** to it. Edexcel expects you to classify sound, electromagnetic, seismic and water waves and explain the difference using these ideas.

core.p: Every wave is a repeating pattern of oscillations. To compare waves (a loud sound with a quiet one, red light with blue light) scientists measure a few key quantities. Learn the definitions exactly, because one-mark definition questions are very common.
bullets: **Frequency** tells you how many waves pass each second.
**Wavelength** tells you the length of one complete wave.
**Amplitude** tells you how far the medium is displaced from rest.
**Period** tells you how long one complete wave takes.
**Wave velocity** (wave speed) tells you how fast energy is transferred by the wave.
A **wavefront** is a line joining matching points of a wave, such as all the crests.
**Displacement** is the distance and direction of a point on the wave from its rest (undisturbed) position.

core.p: Frequency is the **number of complete waves passing a point each second**. It is set by the source: a source that vibrates 50 times a second produces waves with a frequency of 50 Hz.
bullets: Unit: **hertz (Hz)**. 1 Hz = one wave per second.
For sound, higher frequency means a **higher pitch**.
For visible light, frequency determines **colour** (red has the lowest frequency, violet the highest).
Frequency is also the number of oscillations each particle makes per second.
When a wave passes into a new medium its frequency **stays the same**, because it is fixed by the source.

callouts.p: The number of waves passing a point each second, measured in hertz (Hz).

core.p: Wavelength is the **distance from a point on one wave to the equivalent point on the next wave**, for example crest to crest or trough to trough. It is the length of one complete wave cycle.
bullets: Symbol: the Greek letter **lambda**. Unit: **metre (m)**.
On a transverse wave: measure **crest to crest** or **trough to trough**.
On a longitudinal wave: measure from the centre of one **compression** to the centre of the next (or rarefaction to rarefaction).
It is the distance between two adjacent **wavefronts**.
Do NOT measure from a crest to the next trough: that is only half a wavelength.
If several waves are shown, divide the total length by the number of complete waves to get a more accurate value.

callouts.p: The distance from a point on one wave to the equivalent point on the adjacent wave.

core.p: Amplitude is the **maximum displacement of a point on the wave from its undisturbed (rest) position**. On a transverse wave diagram it is the height from the middle line to a crest, NOT from a trough to a crest.
bullets: Unit: **metre (m)** (or cm, mm on diagrams).
Crest to trough distance = **2 x amplitude**.
A larger amplitude means the wave carries **more energy**.
For sound, larger amplitude means a **louder** sound.
For light, larger amplitude means **brighter** light.
Amplitude does not affect the speed, frequency or wavelength of the wave.

callouts.p: The maximum displacement of a point on a wave from its undisturbed position.
Amplitude is measured from the rest position to the crest, never from trough to crest. Halve the crest to trough distance.

core.p: The period is the **time taken for one complete wave to pass a point** (or for one particle to make one complete oscillation). Period and frequency are linked: if 50 waves pass each second, each one takes 1/50 of a second.
bullets: Symbol: **T**. Unit: **second (s)**.
Equation: **period = 1 / frequency**, written T = 1 / f, and rearranged f = 1 / T.
High frequency means a short period; low frequency means a long period.
The period can be read from a **displacement-time graph** as the time from one peak to the next.
Remember to convert ms to s (1 ms = 0.001 s) and kHz to Hz before using T = 1 / f.

callouts.p: The time taken for one complete wave (one complete oscillation) to pass a point.

core.p: Wave velocity (wave speed) is the **speed at which the wave moves through the medium**, which is the speed at which energy is transferred. It is NOT the speed at which the particles themselves oscillate.
bullets: Symbol: **v**. Unit: **metre per second (m/s)**.
It depends on the **medium**: sound travels faster in solids than in liquids, and faster in liquids than in gases.
All electromagnetic waves travel at the same speed in a vacuum, 300 000 000 m/s.
Wave velocity links frequency and wavelength: wave speed = frequency x wavelength (v = f x lambda), covered in the next spec point.
For a given speed, a higher frequency means a shorter wavelength.
Velocity strictly includes direction; at GCSE wave velocity and wave speed are used to mean the same thing for these calculations.

callouts.p: The speed at which energy is transferred by the wave (the speed the wave moves through the medium).

core.p: A **wavefront** is an imaginary line joining all the points on a wave that are at the same stage of their oscillation, such as all the points on one crest. Wavefronts are drawn when looking down on waves from above, for example in a ripple tank.
bullets: Adjacent wavefronts are **one wavelength apart**.
The wave travels **at right angles (perpendicular) to the wavefronts**.
A straight vibrating bar produces **plane (straight)** wavefronts; a point dipper produces **circular** wavefronts.
Wavefront diagrams make it easy to show reflection and refraction later in the topic.
Closer wavefronts mean a shorter wavelength.

callouts.p: A line joining points on a wave that are at the same point in their cycle, for example all the crests.

core.p: In a **transverse** wave the oscillations (vibrations) are **perpendicular (at right angles) to the direction of energy transfer**. If the wave travels left to right, the particles move up and down. Transverse waves have **crests (peaks)** and **troughs**.
bullets: Examples: **all electromagnetic waves** (radio, microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays, gamma rays).
**Ripples on the surface of water** (treated as transverse at GCSE).
**Seismic S waves** (secondary waves).
Waves on a string or rope, and side-to-side waves on a slinky.
Electromagnetic waves can travel through a vacuum; mechanical transverse waves need a medium.
Transverse mechanical waves such as S waves can travel through solids but **not through liquids or gases**.

callouts.p: A wave in which the oscillations are perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer.

core.p: In a **longitudinal** wave the oscillations are **parallel to the direction of energy transfer**. Particles move back and forth along the line the wave travels, making regions squashed together (**compressions**) and regions spread out (**rarefactions**).
bullets: Examples: **sound waves** in air, liquids and solids; **ultrasound**; **seismic P waves** (primary waves); push-pull waves on a slinky.
Longitudinal waves **cannot travel through a vacuum**: they need particles.
They can travel through solids, liquids and gases.
Wavelength = distance between the centres of two adjacent compressions.
Amplitude relates to how much the particles are displaced (how strongly squashed the compressions are).
A longitudinal wave can be drawn as a graph that looks like a transverse wave, but the particles still move parallel to the direction of travel.

callouts.p: A wave in which the oscillations are parallel to the direction of energy transfer.

fig.cap: A longitudinal wave such as sound. Particles vibrate back and forth parallel to the direction of travel, forming compressions and rarefactions. The wavelength is the distance between the centres of adjacent compressions.

core.h: Classifying sound, electromagnetic, seismic and water waves
core.p: The spec names four families of wave you must classify. Learn this table: it is the basis of many one and two mark questions.
bullets: **Sound:** longitudinal. Needs a medium. Travels in solids, liquids and gases.
**Electromagnetic:** transverse. No medium needed; travels through a vacuum.
**Seismic P waves:** longitudinal. Travel through solids and liquids.
**Seismic S waves:** transverse. Travel through solids only.
**Water (surface ripples):** transverse.
A quick test: if the wave can travel through a vacuum, it is electromagnetic and therefore transverse.

callouts.t: P is push, S is shake
callouts.p: P waves are longitudinal (push-pull); S waves are transverse (side to side shake) and cannot pass through liquids.

core.p: Earthquakes release energy as **seismic waves** that travel through the Earth. Detecting them at stations around the world gave scientists information about the Earth's interior.
bullets: **P waves** (primary) are **longitudinal** and travel through both solids and liquids. They are faster, so they arrive first.
**S waves** (secondary) are **transverse** and travel through **solids only**. They are slower.
S waves are not detected on the opposite side of the Earth from an earthquake, which is evidence that the Earth's **outer core is liquid**.
The difference between P and S waves is a direct application of the transverse versus longitudinal distinction.
Surface seismic waves cause most of the shaking damage to buildings.

core.p: Exam questions often ask you to describe the difference. The key is always the direction of the oscillations compared with the direction of energy transfer; everything else follows from this.
bullets: Transverse: oscillations **perpendicular** to energy transfer; has **crests and troughs**.
Longitudinal: oscillations **parallel** to energy transfer; has **compressions and rarefactions**.
Both transfer **energy and information** without transferring matter.
Both have a frequency, wavelength, amplitude, period and wave velocity.
Both obey the same wave equation, v = f x lambda.
A slinky can show both: shake side to side for transverse, push and pull for longitudinal.

callouts.p: Mark schemes want oscillations compared with the direction of energy transfer (or wave travel). Saying the wave moves up and down is not enough.

analogy.t: A queue of people passing on a nudge
analogy.p: Imagine a long queue. If the person at the front gets a shove backwards along the queue and each person bumps the next, the bump travels along the line while everyone just rocks back and forth on the spot: that is a longitudinal wave, with bunched-up people as compressions. If instead each person in turn raises and lowers their arms, the pattern travels along while arms move up and down at right angles to the queue: that is a transverse wave. The number of nudges per second is the frequency, how far each person sways is the amplitude, and the gap between two bunches is the wavelength. Where it breaks down: people react by choice and with delays, while particles are pushed by forces; and electromagnetic waves need no queue of particles at all.

A wave in which the oscillations are parallel to the direction of energy transfer.
A region of a longitudinal wave where particles are pushed closer together.
A region of a longitudinal wave where particles are spread further apart.
A longitudinal seismic wave that can travel through solids and liquids.
A transverse seismic wave that can travel through solids but not liquids.

exam.q: State the unit of frequency.
model: hertz / Hz
exam.tip: Capital H, lower case z.

exam.q: Which of these is a longitudinal wave? A light B microwaves C sound D water ripples
model: C sound
exam.tip: All EM waves are transverse.

exam.q: Define the term frequency.
model: The number of waves passing a point per second
exam.tip: Include per second.

exam.q: Define the term amplitude.
model: The maximum displacement of a point on the wave from its undisturbed / rest position
exam.tip: Use maximum displacement and rest position.

exam.q: A diagram shows a wave with a crest to trough distance of 6.0 cm. 4 complete waves occupy 1.2 m. Determine the amplitude and the wavelength.
model: Amplitude = 6.0 / 2 = 3.0 cm
Wavelength = 1.2 / 4 = 0.30 m
exam.tip: Halve crest to trough; divide total length by number of complete waves.

exam.q: A wave has a frequency of 20 Hz. Calculate its period.
exam.tip: Give the unit, seconds.

exam.q: Describe the difference between transverse and longitudinal waves.
model: In transverse waves the oscillations are perpendicular / at right angles to the direction of energy transfer
In longitudinal waves the oscillations are parallel to the direction of energy transfer
exam.tip: Refer to the direction of energy transfer in both halves.

exam.q: Give one example of a transverse wave and one example of a longitudinal wave.
model: Transverse: any EM wave e.g. light, radio / water ripples / S waves
Longitudinal: sound / ultrasound / P waves
exam.tip: Be specific: wave on its own scores nothing.

exam.q: Explain what is meant by a wavefront and how wavefronts are related to the wavelength and the direction of travel.
model: A line joining points on the wave at the same stage of their cycle (e.g. all crests)
Adjacent wavefronts are one wavelength apart and the wave travels perpendicular to them
exam.tip: Two linked facts: spacing and direction.

exam.q: Seismic waves from an earthquake are detected at stations around the world. Explain how the properties of P and S waves give evidence that part of the Earth's core is liquid.
model: P waves are longitudinal; S waves are transverse
P waves can travel through solids and liquids
S waves can only travel through solids / cannot travel through liquids
S waves are not detected on the opposite side of the Earth, so they must have been stopped by a liquid outer core
exam.tip: Link wave type to what it can travel through, then to the observation.

exam.q: Compare sound waves and light waves, referring to the type of wave and how they travel.
model: Sound is a longitudinal wave; light is a transverse (electromagnetic) wave
In sound, particles oscillate parallel to the direction of energy transfer
Sound has compressions and rarefactions
In light, the oscillations are perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer
Sound needs a medium and cannot travel through a vacuum; light can travel through a vacuum
Light travels much faster (3 x 10^8 m/s) than sound in air (about 340 m/s)
Both transfer energy and information and both have frequency, wavelength and amplitude
exam.tip: Level-marked: give similarities and differences, using the correct terms.

worked.q: A loudspeaker cone vibrates 250 times each second. State the frequency of the sound and calculate its period.
steps: Frequency = number of waves per second = 250 Hz.
Period T = 1 / f

worked.q: A displacement-time graph shows one point on a wave oscillating between +2.5 mm and -2.5 mm, with peaks occurring at 0.010 s and 0.030 s. Find the amplitude, period and frequency.
steps: Amplitude = maximum displacement from rest = 2.5 mm.
Period = time between adjacent peaks = 0.030 - 0.010 = 0.020 s.
f = 50 Hz
worked.ans: Amplitude 2.5 mm, period 0.020 s, frequency 50 Hz

worked.q: On a slinky, the centres of 5 consecutive compressions are spread over 2.0 m. Find the wavelength and state the type of wave.
steps: 5 consecutive compressions contain 4 complete wavelengths between them (count the gaps, not the compressions).
Wavelength = 2.0 / 4 = 0.50 m.
The wave has compressions, and the coils oscillate parallel to the direction of energy transfer.
So it is a longitudinal wave.
worked.ans: 0.50 m; longitudinal

phy_edx.3.10.summary: This core practical asks you to measure the **frequency**, **wavelength** and **speed** of waves in a **fluid** (water waves in a **ripple tank**) and in a **solid** (sound waves in a **metal rod** struck with a hammer), and to judge how **suitable** the equipment is for each measurement. In both cases the speed is found with **v = f × λ**. The grade 9 skill is evaluating: explaining which equipment gives the most accurate readings, why measuring many wavelengths or repeating readings reduces uncertainty, and how to improve the method.

core.p: The practical has two parts: waves on the surface of water (a fluid) and sound waves in a solid rod. In each part you measure two of the three quantities and calculate the third, then evaluate the equipment you used.
bullets: Aim: investigate the **suitability of equipment** to measure the **speed, frequency and wavelength** of a wave in a **solid** and a **fluid**.
Key equation: **wave speed = frequency × wavelength**, v = f × λ.
Speed can also be found with **v = x ÷ t** (distance travelled ÷ time taken).
Units: v in **m/s**, f in **Hz**, λ in **m**, x in **m**, t in **s**.
Convert cm to m before calculating (divide by 100).

core.p: A ripple tank is a shallow, clear-bottomed tray of water. A **vibrating bar (dipper)** driven by a small **motor** connected to a **power supply or signal generator** makes straight plane waves. A **lamp** above the tank shines through the water, and the wave crests act like lenses, so a pattern of **bright and dark lines** (shadows of the wavefronts) appears on a **white screen or card** below.

**Vibrating bar** (dipper) just touching the water surface.
**Motor** and **power supply / signal generator** to set the frequency.
**Lamp** above the tank; **white card** or screen below.
**Metre rule** or ruler on the card; **stopwatch**; optionally a **camera/phone** or a **stroboscope**.

callouts.p: It is hard to measure waves on the water directly. The shadow pattern on the card is larger and stationary relative to a ruler, so measurements are easier.

core.h: Part 1 method: measuring wavelength, frequency and speed
core.p: Switch on the motor and adjust the frequency so the waves are clearly visible and not too fast to count. Then take each measurement in the way that keeps the uncertainty smallest.
bullets: **Wavelength**: place a ruler on the screen; measure the distance across a number of bright lines, e.g. **10 wavelengths**, then **divide by 10**.
Taking a **photo** (or video still) with the ruler in shot freezes the pattern, so you can measure more accurately.
**Frequency**: count the number of waves passing a fixed point in **10 s**, then **divide by 10**; or read the frequency from the **signal generator**.
Filming the waves and counting in **slow motion** removes the problem of waves being too fast to count.
**Speed** method 1: **v = f × λ** using your two measurements.
**Speed** method 2: time how long one wavefront takes to travel a measured distance across the tank, then **v = distance ÷ time**.
**Repeat** each measurement and calculate a **mean**; compare the speeds from the two methods.

callouts.p: Measuring across 10 wavelengths, or counting waves for 10 s, spreads the same ruler or timing uncertainty over many waves, so the percentage uncertainty in one wavelength or one period is much smaller.

core.h: Part 2 apparatus: sound waves in a solid rod
core.p: A long **metal rod** is supported horizontally, for example held in **clamp stands** or hung by rubber bands near its ends so it can vibrate freely. Striking one end with a **hammer** sets up a sound wave that travels along the rod and reflects back and forth. A **microphone** connected to a **frequency app**, computer or **oscilloscope** measures the frequency of the loud note produced.
bullets: **Metal rod** (about 1 m long), supported so it can vibrate freely.
**Hammer** to strike the end of the rod.
**Microphone** connected to a **frequency app** on a phone/computer, or an **oscilloscope**.
**Metre rule** or tape measure to measure the **length of the rod**.
The rod vibrates mainly at the frequency where its **length is half a wavelength**, so **λ = 2 × length of rod**.

callouts.p: For the main note, the rod length equals half a wavelength, so wavelength = 2 × rod length. You are not expected to measure the wavelength directly.

core.h: Part 2 method: measuring the speed of sound in the rod
core.p: Follow a clear sequence so each reading is taken under the same conditions, then repeat to check the results are repeatable.
bullets: Measure the **length of the rod** with a metre rule.
Support the rod so it can vibrate freely and place the **microphone** near one end.
Strike the end of the rod **firmly** with the hammer.
Read the **peak frequency** of the note from the app or oscilloscope.
**Repeat** several times and calculate the **mean frequency**; discard anomalous readings.
Calculate **λ = 2 × length**, then **v = f × λ**.
Typical result: several thousand metres per second (for example about 5000 m/s in steel or aluminium), much faster than sound in air.

callouts.p: With an oscilloscope, measure the time period T of one wave from the trace (squares × time-base setting) and use f = 1 ÷ T.

core.p: Even though this is a measuring practical rather than a cause-and-effect investigation, you should be able to identify what is kept the same to make results valid.
bullets: Ripple tank: keep the **water depth constant** (and the tank **level**), because the speed of water waves depends on depth.
Ripple tank: keep the **frequency setting** the same while measuring wavelength and frequency for one result.
Rod: use the **same rod** (same material and length) and strike the **same place** each time.
Rod: keep the **microphone position** the same.
Measured: wavelength and frequency (fluid); frequency and length (solid). Calculated: speed.

callouts.p: Water waves travel more slowly in shallower water. If the tank is not level, the wavelength changes across the tank and your measurement is inaccurate.

core.p: This is the heart of the practical. For each measurement, think about the **resolution** of the instrument, the size of the quantity, and sources of **random** and **systematic** error. Suitable equipment gives a small percentage uncertainty compared with the size of the reading.
bullets: **Ruler on the screen**: mm resolution is fine for a 15 cm span of 10 waves, but poor for a single 1.5 cm wavelength (large percentage uncertainty).
**Moving waves** are hard to measure: a **photo with a ruler** or a **stroboscope** (set so the waves appear frozen) is more suitable.
**Counting waves by eye** works only at **low frequency**; at high frequency waves are too fast to count, so use the **signal generator reading** or a **slow-motion video**.
**Stopwatch** timing has **human reaction time** error (about 0.2 to 0.3 s); timing for a longer period (10 s or more) makes this error a smaller fraction of the reading.
**Microphone and frequency app** is very suitable for the rod: sound is too fast (thousands of m/s) to time with a stopwatch over 1 m, and too high in frequency to count.
**Metre rule** for the rod length is suitable: about 1 m measured to 1 mm is a tiny percentage uncertainty.
Measuring the **speed of sound in a rod with a stopwatch** would be unsuitable: the time over 1 m is less than a millisecond, far smaller than reaction time.

head: Measurement
Equipment
Suitability and improvement
rows: measure across 10 waves; photograph with ruler
count for 10 s; use slow-motion video or signal generator
stopwatch and ruler, or v = f × λ
time over a longer distance; compare two methods
very suitable; repeat and take mean

callouts.p: Equipment is suitable when its resolution and the method give a small percentage uncertainty compared with the size of the measurement.

core.p: Know the difference between the types of error and how each improvement works, because the mark schemes reward the reason as well as the improvement.
bullets: **Random error**: readings scatter (e.g. counting, reaction time, parallax). Reduce by **repeating and averaging** and by measuring over **many waves**.
**Systematic error**: every reading is off by the same amount (e.g. ruler zero error, screen pattern magnified). Reduce by **calibrating** or correcting the method.
**Parallax error**: read the ruler with your eye **level** and **perpendicular** to the scale.

The shadow pattern on the screen is **magnified** slightly compared with the real waves because the light spreads out from the lamp; for accurate real wavelengths, keep the screen close or calibrate with an object of known size.
**Anomalous results** should be identified and repeated or left out of the mean.
Use the **mean** of repeat readings and quote the answer to a sensible number of significant figures.

callouts.p: Do not just say 'repeat it'. Say 'repeat and calculate a mean to reduce the effect of random errors'.

core.p: Risks are low but examiners like specific hazards with specific control measures.
bullets: **Water and electricity**: keep the power supply and lamp away from water; mop up spills immediately.
**Hot lamp**: do not touch the lamp; allow to cool.
**Stroboscope**: flashing light can trigger photosensitive epilepsy; check with the class first.
**Hammer**: strike gently and keep fingers clear; make sure the rod is secure so it cannot fall.
**Loud noise**: strike the rod gently to avoid an uncomfortably loud sound.

core.h: Processing results and comparing fluid with solid
core.p: When you have your values, calculate the speed, compare repeat values and compare the two media. Sound in a solid is thousands of times faster than water ripples, which is why completely different equipment is needed for each.
bullets: Ripple tank waves: typically speeds of a few **tens of centimetres per second**.
Sound in a metal rod: typically **thousands of metres per second**.
Fast waves need **electronic** measurement (microphone, app, oscilloscope); slow waves can be measured with **rulers, stopwatches and cameras**.
Compare speeds from the two ripple tank methods: if they agree closely, the results are more **reliable** (repeatable and accurate).

callouts.p: The speed and frequency of the wave decide the equipment: slow, low-frequency waves suit manual methods; fast, high-frequency waves need electronic sensors.

analogy.p: Finding wave speed is like measuring traffic. For slow cars on a car park road (ripples) you can stand with a stopwatch and tape measure. For racing cars (sound in a rod) a stopwatch is useless, so you need electronic sensors. Measuring the gap over ten cars and dividing by ten gives a better average gap than measuring one gap. The analogy breaks down because in a wave nothing physically travels along like a car: only energy moves, while the water or metal particles just oscillate about fixed positions.

terms.d: A shallow clear tray of water used to produce and observe water waves, with a lamp above and screen below.
A bar driven by a motor that touches the water surface and makes straight (plane) waves.
A device that supplies an alternating signal of a chosen frequency, used to set the vibration frequency.
A light that flashes at an adjustable rate; when it matches the wave frequency the waves appear stationary.
The number of waves passing a point each second, measured in hertz (Hz).
The distance from one point on a wave to the same point on the next wave, e.g. crest to crest.
The distance travelled by a wave each second; v = f × λ.
The time for one complete wave to pass a point; T = 1 ÷ f.
An instrument that displays a signal as a trace on a screen so its period and frequency can be measured.
The smallest change in a quantity that a measuring instrument can detect.
Unpredictable variation in readings that causes them to spread around the true value; reduced by repeating and averaging.
An error that shifts every reading by the same amount in the same direction, e.g. a zero error.
The range within which the true value is likely to lie.
How close a measurement is to the true value.
When the same person repeats the experiment with the same method and equipment and gets similar results.
A substance that can flow: a liquid or a gas.

mistakes.w: Measure one wavelength with a ruler.
mistakes.r: Measure across several (e.g. 10) wavelengths and divide by the number of waves to reduce uncertainty.

mistakes.w: Repeat it to make it more accurate.
mistakes.r: Repeat and calculate a mean to reduce the effect of random errors.

mistakes.w: Use a stopwatch to time sound travelling along the rod.
mistakes.r: The time is far too short for a stopwatch (reaction time); use a microphone and frequency app/oscilloscope and v = f × λ.

mistakes.w: The wavelength in the rod equals the length of the rod.
mistakes.r: The length of the rod is half a wavelength, so wavelength = 2 × length.

mistakes.w: Speed = frequency ÷ wavelength.
mistakes.r: Speed = frequency × wavelength (v = f × λ).

mistakes.w: Using the wavelength in cm with speed in m/s.
mistakes.r: Convert cm to m (divide by 100) before using v = f × λ.

mistakes.w: Count the waves passing a point for 1 second.
mistakes.r: Count for a longer time (e.g. 10 s) and divide, to reduce the effect of reaction time and counting errors.

mistakes.w: Safety: be careful with water.
mistakes.r: Keep electrical equipment (power supply, lamp) away from the water and wipe up spills, to avoid electric shock.

exam.q: State the equation linking wave speed, frequency and wavelength.
model: wave speed = frequency × wavelength (v = f × λ)
exam.tip: This equation must be recalled.

exam.q: Describe how a student could use a ripple tank to measure the wavelength of water waves accurately.
model: Measure the distance across several (e.g. 10) waves/bright lines on the screen using a ruler
divide by the number of waves (or photograph the pattern with a ruler to measure it)
exam.tip: Always include 'divide by the number of waves'.

exam.q: Describe how the frequency of the water waves can be measured.
model: Count the number of waves passing a fixed point in a measured time, e.g. 10 s
divide the number of waves by the time
exam.tip: Or state reading from the signal generator.

exam.q: Explain why the student measured the time for 20 waves rather than for 1 wave.
model: The time for one wave is very short / reaction time is large compared with it
timing many waves reduces the percentage uncertainty / effect of reaction time
exam.tip: Link to reaction time.

exam.q: A student finds that 10 wavelengths on the screen measure 18.0 cm and that 40 waves pass a point in 10 s. Calculate the wave speed in m/s.
model: wavelength = 18.0 ÷ 10 = 1.8 cm = 0.018 m
frequency = 40 ÷ 10 = 4.0 Hz
exam.tip: Convert to metres before multiplying.

exam.q: A metal rod of length 0.80 m produces a note of frequency 3100 Hz when struck. The wavelength is twice the length of the rod. Calculate the speed of sound in the rod.
exam.tip: Find λ first.

exam.q: Explain why a microphone and frequency app is more suitable than a stopwatch for finding the speed of sound in a metal rod.
model: Sound travels so fast in a solid that the time to travel along the rod is far too short to measure with a stopwatch (reaction time)
the app measures the high frequency directly/accurately, so v = f × λ can be used
exam.tip: Compare the time involved with human reaction time.

exam.q: Suggest why the ripple tank should be level.
model: So the depth of water is the same everywhere
because wave speed (and so wavelength) depends on depth
exam.tip: Mention speed depends on depth.

exam.q: Give one hazard in the ripple tank experiment and a way to reduce the risk.
model: Water near electrical equipment / mains lamp could cause electric shock
keep electrical equipment away from water and mop up spills immediately
exam.tip: Hazard plus specific control.

exam.q: Evaluate the suitability of the equipment used to measure the speed, frequency and wavelength of waves in a ripple tank and in a solid rod, and suggest improvements.
model: Ripple tank wavelength: ruler on screen is suitable if measured over many waves; single wavelength gives large percentage uncertainty
moving pattern hard to measure: photograph with a ruler or use a stroboscope to freeze it
frequency by counting is only suitable at low frequency; use slow-motion video or the signal generator
stopwatch timing affected by reaction time; time over longer periods/distances and repeat for a mean
rod: speed too high for stopwatch timing, so microphone with frequency app/oscilloscope is suitable
metre rule suitable for rod length (small percentage uncertainty); wavelength = 2 × length; v = f × λ
repeat readings, discard anomalies and calculate means to reduce random error
exam.tip: Cover both media, give a judgement for each instrument and an improvement with a reason.

worked.q: In a ripple tank, a student photographs the screen with a ruler. 8 wavelengths span 12.0 cm. A video shows 30 waves pass a mark in 6.0 s. Calculate the wavelength, frequency and speed.
steps: Wavelength = 12.0 cm ÷ 8 = 1.5 cm = 0.015 m
Frequency = 30 waves ÷ 6.0 s = 5.0 Hz

worked.q: A 1.20 m aluminium rod is struck four times. The frequency app gives 2090 Hz, 2080 Hz, 2350 Hz and 2070 Hz. Calculate the speed of sound in the rod.
steps: Identify the anomaly: 2350 Hz is far from the others, so leave it out
Wavelength = 2 × length = 2 × 1.20 = 2.40 m
worked.ans: About 4990 m/s (about 5000 m/s).

worked.q: Model answer: Explain why measuring the speed of a ripple with a stopwatch over a 10 cm distance is less suitable than over 40 cm.
steps: The ripple takes only a short time to travel 10 cm.
Reaction time (about 0.2 s) is then a large fraction of the measured time, so the percentage uncertainty is large.
Over 40 cm the time is about four times longer, so the same reaction time error is a smaller percentage.
So the longer distance gives a more accurate speed; repeating and averaging improves it further.
worked.ans: Timing over a longer distance makes the reaction time error a smaller fraction of the reading, so the speed is more accurate.

phy_edx.3.2.summary: Every wave, whether it is sound, a ripple on water or light, obeys two equations you must recall: **wave speed = frequency × wavelength (v = f λ)** and **wave speed = distance ÷ time (v = x / t)**. The first links the speed to the properties of the wave itself, while the second treats the wave like any moving object covering a distance in a time. Grade 9 answers rearrange both confidently, convert units such as kHz, MHz, cm and km into SI units first, and explain why the equations work.

core.p: Edexcel requires you to **recall and use** both equations for **all waves** (sound, water waves, waves on strings and all electromagnetic waves). They are not given on the equation sheet, so they must be learnt word for word, including the units.
bullets: **wave speed (m/s) = frequency (Hz) × wavelength (m)**, written **v = f λ**
**wave speed (m/s) = distance (m) ÷ time (s)**, written **v = x / t**
v is wave speed in **metres per second (m/s)**
f is frequency in **hertz (Hz)**, where 1 Hz = one wave per second
λ (the Greek letter lambda) is wavelength in **metres (m)**
x is the distance travelled by the wave in **metres (m)** and t is the time taken in **seconds (s)**
Both equations give the same speed for the same wave: they are two different ways of measuring one quantity

callouts.p: The distance travelled by a wave (by a wavefront or a crest) each second.
Both v = f λ and v = x / t are on the list of equations you must recall. They are NOT printed on the Physics equation sheet.

core.p: When a wave travels, the **energy and the wave pattern** move forward but the particles of the medium only oscillate about fixed positions. Wave speed is the speed at which the **pattern** (a crest, a compression or a wavefront) moves through the medium, not the speed of the particles.
bullets: Follow one crest of a water wave: the distance it moves in one second is the wave speed
The water itself only bobs **up and down** (transverse wave); the air in a sound wave only moves **back and forth** (longitudinal wave)
Wave speed depends on the **medium** (what the wave travels through), not on how hard you make the wave
Sound in air is about **330 to 340 m/s**; ripples in a ripple tank are typically **0.1 to 0.3 m/s**; all electromagnetic waves in a vacuum travel at **3 × 10^8 m/s**

callouts.t: Particles do not travel with the wave
callouts.p: Never write that particles move at the wave speed. The wave transfers energy and information, not matter.

core.p: To use v = f λ you must be sure what f and λ mean. These are defined in spec points 4.3 to 4.5, but you need them here to plug in the right numbers.
bullets: **Frequency** is the number of waves passing a point **each second**
**Wavelength** is the distance from one point on a wave to the **same point on the next wave**, for example crest to crest or compression to compression
**Period** is the time for **one complete wave** to pass a point
Period and frequency are linked by **T = 1 / f**, so a 50 Hz wave has a period of 1 / 50 = 0.02 s
Measure wavelength crest to crest, never crest to trough (that is only half a wavelength)

callouts.p: The distance from a point on one wave to the equivalent point on the adjacent wave.
The number of waves passing a point each second.

fig.cap: A transverse wave. The wavelength λ is measured from one crest to the next crest. The frequency f is how many of these complete waves pass a fixed point each second, and the whole pattern moves to the right at the wave speed v.

core.p: This is the reasoning examiners love in higher-mark answers. Think about a fixed point that the wave is passing. Each second, **f complete waves** pass that point, and each wave is **λ metres long**. So in one second the wave pattern moves forward f lots of λ, which is a distance of f × λ metres. Distance travelled per second is speed, so **v = f λ**.
bullets: Example: if 4 waves pass each second and each is 2 m long, the front of the wave moves 4 × 2 = 8 m every second, so v = 8 m/s
Another way: in one **period T** the wave moves forward exactly **one wavelength λ**, so v = λ / T; since T = 1 / f this becomes v = f λ
This links v = f λ directly to v = x / t (distance λ in time T)
So the two wave equations are really the same idea: speed is distance divided by time

callouts.p: If asked to explain the equation, say: f waves pass per second, each of length λ, so the distance the wave travels per second (its speed) is f × λ.

core.p: You must be able to make any of the three quantities the subject. A formula triangle helps, but grade 9 students also rearrange algebraically so they can check each step.
bullets: **v = f × λ** to find speed
**f = v ÷ λ** to find frequency
**λ = v ÷ f** to find wavelength
Check the answer is sensible: for a fixed speed, a **higher frequency means a shorter wavelength**
For a fixed speed, f and λ are **inversely proportional**: doubling f halves λ

callouts.p: In the same medium the wave speed stays the same, so if the frequency increases, the wavelength must decrease by the same factor.

core.h: Using v = x / t for waves
core.p: Waves travel through a medium at a steady speed, so you can treat a wave pulse or wavefront like a car on a road. Measure how far it travels (x) and how long it takes (t), then divide.
bullets: **v = x ÷ t** to find speed
**x = v × t** to find distance
**t = x ÷ v** to find time
Used for: thunder after lightning, a ripple crossing a tank, a sound pulse between two microphones, seismic waves reaching a station, radio signals from a spacecraft
Because light is so fast (3 × 10^8 m/s), the time for light to cross a few hundred metres is negligible, which is why we see lightning almost instantly but hear thunder later

callouts.p: In v = x / t, x is the total distance travelled by the wave, not the wavelength and not the amplitude.

core.p: Most lost marks in wave calculations come from units. Both equations only work in **SI units**: metres, seconds, hertz and metres per second. Convert every value before substituting.
bullets: **kHz to Hz**: multiply by 1000 (2.5 kHz = 2500 Hz)
**MHz to Hz**: multiply by 1 000 000 (100 MHz = 1.0 × 10^8 Hz)
**GHz to Hz**: multiply by 1 000 000 000 (2.4 GHz = 2.4 × 10^9 Hz)
**cm to m**: divide by 100 (4.0 cm = 0.040 m)
**mm to m**: divide by 1000 (5 mm = 0.005 m)
**km to m**: multiply by 1000 (1.7 km = 1700 m)
**ms to s**: divide by 1000; **minutes to s**: multiply by 60
Electromagnetic wave questions often need standard form: write 3 × 10^8 as 3E8 or 3 × 10^8 on your calculator using the ×10^x button

callouts.p: Write the unit next to every number in your substitution line. If you see cm or kHz, stop and convert.

core.p: Examiners award marks for the method, so set your working out the same way every time. Even if your final answer is wrong, a correct substitution usually earns a mark.
bullets: 1. **Write down** what you know with units, and what you want to find
2. **Choose** the equation: if you are given f or λ, use v = f λ; if you are given a distance and a time, use v = x / t
3. **Convert** to SI units
4. **Rearrange** before substituting (or substitute then rearrange, both are accepted)
5. **Substitute** the numbers
6. **Calculate** and give the answer with the **correct unit** and sensible significant figures (usually the same as the data, often 2 or 3)
Some questions need **both** equations: for example find v from x and t, then use that v to find λ from f

callouts.p: Writing the equation in symbols or words is often the first marking point, especially in 3 and 4 mark calculations.

core.h: What changes the speed, and what does not
core.p: A very common higher-tier idea: the **medium** sets the speed of a wave and the **source** sets its frequency. Knowing which is which lets you predict what happens to wavelength.
bullets: Changing the frequency of a signal generator does **not** change the speed of sound in air, so the wavelength changes instead (λ = v ÷ f)
Water waves travel **slower in shallow water** than in deep water; the frequency stays the same, so the wavelength gets **shorter** in shallow water
When a wave crosses into a new medium its **frequency stays the same** (each wave that arrives at the boundary leaves it), so any change in speed causes a matching change in wavelength
Sound travels faster in solids and liquids than in gases, so sound of a given frequency has a longer wavelength in water than in air
All electromagnetic waves have the same speed in a vacuum, so for EM waves a higher frequency always means a shorter wavelength

callouts.t: Frequency is fixed by the source
callouts.p: Frequency does not change when a wave changes medium. Speed and wavelength change together.

core.h: Typical wave speeds to sense-check answers
core.p: Knowing roughly how fast waves travel lets you spot a calculator or unit slip immediately.
bullets: Sound in air: about **330 to 340 m/s** (a value of 340 m/s is common in questions)
Sound in water: about **1500 m/s**
Sound in steel: about **5000 to 6000 m/s**
Ripples in a ripple tank: roughly **0.1 to 0.3 m/s**
Ocean waves: a few m/s
Light and all electromagnetic waves in a vacuum: **300 000 000 m/s = 3 × 10^8 m/s**
If you get sound in air at 34 000 m/s or 3.4 m/s, you have probably forgotten to convert cm to m

callouts.t: Do not invent the speed of light
callouts.p: Use the value the question gives. If none is given for EM waves, use 3 × 10^8 m/s.

core.h: Applying the equations to electromagnetic waves
core.p: The equations apply to all waves, including radio, microwaves and light. These questions look scary because of the powers of ten but use exactly the same method.
bullets: A radio station broadcasting at 100 MHz: λ = v ÷ f = 3 × 10^8 ÷ 1 × 10^8 = **3 m**
Time for a radio signal to travel 3.6 × 10^7 m to a satellite: t = x ÷ v = 3.6 × 10^7 ÷ 3 × 10^8 = **0.12 s**
Give answers in standard form when the numbers are very large or very small

core.h: Reading wave data from graphs and diagrams
core.p: Exam questions often hide f or λ in a diagram rather than giving the number directly.
bullets: A diagram showing **several wavelengths** over a distance: divide the total distance by the number of complete waves to get λ
A **displacement against time** graph: the horizontal distance for one cycle is the **period T**, so f = 1 / T
A **displacement against distance** graph: one cycle is the **wavelength λ**
Check the axis label carefully: time axis gives T, distance axis gives λ
Counting: 5 waves passing in 2 s gives f = 5 ÷ 2 = 2.5 Hz

callouts.p: Measuring across several wavelengths and dividing gives a more accurate wavelength than measuring just one.

analogy.p: Imagine a marching band walking past you. The number of rows passing you each second is the frequency, the gap from the front of one row to the front of the next is the wavelength, and the speed of the band is rows per second × gap per row, exactly like v = f λ. Timing how long the band takes to march the length of the street is like v = x / t. Where it breaks down: in a real wave the particles do not march along with the wave; they only oscillate about fixed positions while the pattern and energy move forward. Also, a band can choose to walk faster, but a wave's speed is set by the medium, not by the source.

terms.d: The distance travelled by a wave each second, measured in metres per second (m/s).
The number of waves passing a point each second, measured in hertz (Hz).
The unit of frequency; 1 Hz is one wave (one cycle) per second.
The distance from a point on one wave to the equivalent point on the adjacent wave, measured in metres (m).
The time taken for one complete wave to pass a point, measured in seconds; T = 1 / f.
The total distance travelled by a wave, in metres, used in v = x / t.
The time taken for the wave to travel the distance x, in seconds.
The substance a wave travels through, such as air, water or a solid; it determines the wave speed.
A line joining points on a wave that are at the same point in their cycle, for example along a crest.
The highest point of a transverse wave above the rest position.
The lowest point of a transverse wave below the rest position.
When one quantity doubles the other halves; for a fixed wave speed, frequency and wavelength are inversely proportional.
The standard units used in equations: metres, seconds, hertz and metres per second for wave calculations.
The speed of all electromagnetic waves in a vacuum, 3 × 10^8 m/s.

mistakes.w: Uses a wavelength given in cm (or frequency in kHz) directly in v = f λ.
mistakes.r: Convert to SI units first: cm ÷ 100 to get m, kHz × 1000 to get Hz.

mistakes.w: Measures wavelength from a crest to the next trough.
mistakes.r: Wavelength is crest to crest (or the same point on adjacent waves); crest to trough is half a wavelength.

mistakes.w: Writes v = f ÷ λ or λ = f ÷ v.
mistakes.r: v = f × λ, so f = v ÷ λ and λ = v ÷ f.

mistakes.w: Says increasing the frequency of a sound increases its speed.
mistakes.r: The speed is set by the medium and stays the same; increasing frequency decreases the wavelength.

mistakes.w: States that the frequency changes when a wave enters a new medium.
mistakes.r: Frequency stays the same; speed and wavelength change.

mistakes.w: Gives the answer without a unit, or with Hz for a speed.
mistakes.r: Speed in m/s, frequency in Hz, wavelength in m.

mistakes.w: Uses the wavelength as x in v = x / t.
mistakes.r: x is the total distance the wave travels in time t.

mistakes.w: Reads the period from a displacement against distance graph.
mistakes.r: A displacement against distance graph gives wavelength; a displacement against time graph gives period, and f = 1 / T.

mistakes.w: Says the particles of the medium travel at the wave speed.
mistakes.r: The wave pattern and energy travel at the wave speed; particles only oscillate about fixed positions.

exam.q: State the equation linking wave speed, frequency and wavelength.
model: wave speed = frequency × wavelength (v = f λ)
exam.tip: Words or correct symbols both score; do not write it as a formula triangle only.

exam.q: State the equation linking wave speed, distance and time.
model: wave speed = distance ÷ time (v = x / t)
exam.tip: Avoid writing distance = speed ÷ time, which is a common slip.

exam.q: A water wave has a frequency of 2.0 Hz and a wavelength of 0.15 m. Calculate the speed of the wave.
exam.tip: Substitution then answer with unit.

exam.q: A sound wave travels at 340 m/s in air. Its frequency is 680 Hz. Calculate its wavelength.
exam.tip: Rearrange carefully: wavelength is speed divided by frequency.

exam.q: A radio station transmits at 97.5 MHz. Radio waves travel at 3.0 × 10^8 m/s. Calculate the wavelength of the radio waves.
exam.tip: The MHz conversion is usually worth a mark of its own.

exam.q: Thunder is heard 3.0 s after a lightning flash. The speed of sound in air is 340 m/s. Calculate the distance to the lightning.
model: x = v × t
exam.tip: The light arrives almost instantly, so the 3.0 s is the sound travel time.

exam.q: A ripple takes 4.0 s to travel across a ripple tank 0.60 m long. Calculate the speed of the ripple.
exam.tip: Use v = x / t when you are given a distance and a time.

exam.q: A student increases the frequency of a sound from a loudspeaker while the speed of sound stays the same. Explain what happens to the wavelength of the sound.
model: wavelength decreases
because v = f λ and v is constant, so λ is inversely proportional to f (λ = v ÷ f)
exam.tip: Always link the answer to the equation and say which quantity is constant.

exam.q: Explain why wave speed = frequency × wavelength.
model: frequency is the number of waves passing a point each second
each wave has length λ, so the distance the wave travels per second (speed) is f × λ
exam.tip: Think distance per second.

exam.q: Water waves travel from deep water into shallow water. Their speed decreases from 1.2 m/s to 0.80 m/s. The frequency of the waves is 0.40 Hz. Calculate the change in wavelength and explain why the frequency does not change.
model: wavelength in deep water = 1.2 ÷ 0.40 = 3.0 m
wavelength in shallow water = 0.80 ÷ 0.40 = 2.0 m
decrease of 1.0 m
frequency is set by the source / the same number of waves arrive at and leave the boundary each second
exam.tip: Work out both wavelengths separately, then subtract.

exam.q: A sound pulse travels 1.7 km through air in 5.0 s. The sound has a frequency of 850 Hz. Calculate the wavelength of the sound.
exam.tip: Two-step questions: find v with v = x / t, then use v = f λ.

exam.q: Describe how the speed of a wave can be found using v = f λ and using v = x / t, and explain why both methods should give the same value.
model: v = f λ: find the frequency (count waves passing a point per second or read it from the source)
measure the wavelength (measure across several waves and divide)
multiply frequency by wavelength
v = x / t: measure the distance a wavefront or pulse travels and the time taken, then divide
in one period T the wave travels one wavelength, so v = λ / T
since f = 1 / T, λ / T = f λ, so both equations describe the same speed
exam.tip: Six mark answers need both methods and the link between them.

worked.q: A wave on a string has a frequency of 25 Hz and a wavelength of 48 cm. Calculate its speed.
steps: Known: f = 25 Hz, λ = 48 cm. Want: v.
Equation: v = f × λ.
Substitute: v = 25 × 0.48.
Calculate: v = 12 m/s.
worked.ans: v = 12 m/s

worked.q: A mobile phone signal has a frequency of 1.8 GHz. Electromagnetic waves travel at 3.0 × 10^8 m/s. Calculate the wavelength.
steps: Known: f = 1.8 GHz, v = 3.0 × 10^8 m/s. Want: λ.
Convert: 1.8 GHz = 1.8 × 10^9 Hz.
Rearrange: λ = v ÷ f.
worked.ans: λ = 0.17 m (about 17 cm)

worked.q: During a storm a student sees lightning and hears the thunder 4.5 s later. The storm is 1.53 km away. Calculate the speed of sound, then calculate the wavelength of a 255 Hz rumble of the thunder.
steps: v = 1530 ÷ 4.5 = 340 m/s (light time is negligible because light travels at 3 × 10^8 m/s).
Step 2, v = f λ rearranged: λ = v ÷ f.
worked.ans: v = 340 m/s and λ = 1.3 m

phy_edx.3.3.summary: Edexcel expects you to **describe how to measure the speed of sound in air and the speed of ripples on a water surface**. Every method comes down to one of two equations: time a wave over a measured distance and use **v = x / t**, or measure the frequency and wavelength and use **v = f λ**. Grade 9 answers give a clear, ordered method, name the equipment, explain how to reduce errors such as human reaction time, and show how the final speed is calculated.

core.h: What the spec wants you to be able to do
core.p: This point is about **experimental methods**. You must be able to describe, step by step, how to measure the velocity of sound waves in air and of ripples on water, and explain how each measurement leads to a speed. Six mark method questions on this are very common.
bullets: Two routes to a speed: **v = x / t** (distance and time) or **v = f λ** (frequency and wavelength)
For sound in air the usual methods are the **echo method**, the **flash and bang method**, and **electronic timing with microphones**
For water ripples the usual apparatus is a **ripple tank** with a vibrating bar, lamp and screen
Expected results: sound in air about **330 to 340 m/s**; ripples in a ripple tank about **0.1 to 0.3 m/s**
Examiners reward: equipment named, what is measured, how it is measured accurately, how the speed is calculated

callouts.p: Every method in this topic uses either v = x / t or v = f λ. Always say which one, and what you measured to use it.

core.h: Why sound is hard to time by hand
core.p: Sound in air travels about 340 metres every second. Over a school-sized distance such as 50 m, sound takes only about 0.15 s. A typical **human reaction time is about 0.2 to 0.3 s**, which is longer than the time being measured. That is why hand-timed methods need **large distances**, **many repeats**, or a trick such as timing lots of echoes together.
bullets: Reaction time adds a **random error** each time a stopwatch is started or stopped
Making the distance bigger makes the time bigger, so the reaction time is a **smaller fraction** of it
Timing many events in one go (for example 20 echoes) spreads one reaction-time error over all of them
Electronic timing with microphones removes reaction time completely, so short distances can then be used

callouts.p: Say WHY an improvement works: a longer distance gives a longer time, so the percentage error caused by reaction time is smaller.

core.h: Method 1: the echo method (sound in air)
core.p: An echo is a sound **reflected** from a hard surface. Stand a measured distance from a large, flat wall and make a sharp sound. The sound travels to the wall **and back**, so the distance travelled is **twice** the distance to the wall.
bullets: Stand at least **50 m** from a large flat wall (such as a sports hall wall) with open space around
Measure the distance d to the wall with a **trundle wheel** or long tape measure
Make a sharp sound by **clapping** or banging two blocks of wood together
Better version: **clap in rhythm** so that each clap is made exactly when the echo of the previous clap is heard
A second person starts a stopwatch on one clap and stops it after counting, for example, **20 intervals**
Time between claps = total time ÷ 20; this is the time for sound to travel **2d**
Speed of sound **v = 2d ÷ t**
Repeat several times and calculate a **mean**

callouts.t: Do not forget the factor of 2
callouts.p: In an echo method the sound goes there and back, so the distance travelled is 2 × the distance to the wall.

core.h: Method 2: the flash and bang method (sound in air)
core.p: Two people stand a long, measured distance apart in an open field. One makes a sound that is also **seen**, such as banging two cymbals together or firing a starting pistol. The other starts a stopwatch on **seeing** the action and stops it on **hearing** the sound.
bullets: Use a large distance, for example **400 to 500 m**, measured with a trundle wheel or a map
Light travels at **3 × 10^8 m/s**, so it crosses 500 m in about 0.000002 s: its travel time is **negligible**
So the time between seeing and hearing is the time for the **sound** to travel the distance
Speed of sound **v = x / t**
Repeat many times and take a **mean**; discard anomalous results
Swap positions and repeat, so that any effect of **wind** blowing one way is averaged out
Using several timers at once and averaging their readings reduces random error

callouts.p: Light is almost a million times faster than sound, so seeing the action is effectively an instant start signal.

core.h: Method 3: two microphones and electronic timing
core.p: Electronic timing removes reaction time, so the distance can be just a metre or two. Two microphones are placed a measured distance apart in a line with the sound source and connected to a **datalogger, fast timer or oscilloscope**.
bullets: Place two microphones a measured distance apart (for example **1.00 m**) using a metre rule
Make a sharp sound (clap or hammer tap) in line with both microphones, beyond the first one
The timer **starts** when the sound reaches the first microphone and **stops** when it reaches the second
The timer shows the time t for sound to travel between the microphones
Speed of sound **v = x / t**, where x is the distance between the microphones
Repeat, and repeat at different distances; plotting distance against time gives a straight line whose **gradient is the speed**

Alternative using v = f λ: connect a loudspeaker to a **signal generator** of known frequency, display both microphone signals on an **oscilloscope**, move one microphone until the traces are **in step**, then move it further until they are in step again; the distance moved is **one wavelength**

callouts.p: A graph of distance travelled against time taken uses many results at once, so it reduces the effect of random errors in any single reading.

core.p: A ripple tank is a shallow, transparent tray of water used to make and see **water waves (ripples)**. A **lamp above** the tank shines down through the water; the wave crests act like lenses and focus the light, so a pattern of **bright and dark lines** (the wavefronts) appears on a white sheet of paper or screen **below** the tank.
bullets: A **vibrating bar** (a dipper attached to a small electric motor) touches the surface and makes straight (plane) waves; a ball-shaped dipper makes circular waves
The **frequency** of the waves equals the frequency at which the bar vibrates, controlled by the power supply
Keep the **water depth the same** all over the tank (about 1 cm), because ripples travel slower in shallower water
The shadow pattern on the paper lets you see and measure the waves without disturbing the water
Placing a **ruler** on the paper (or in the picture) gives a scale for measuring wavelength

core.p: One wavelength of a ripple is only a centimetre or two, so measuring a single gap gives a large percentage error. Instead measure across **many wavefronts** and divide.
bullets: Place a metre rule (or ruler) at right angles to the wavefronts on the paper
Measure the distance across, for example, **10 complete wavelengths** (11 bright lines)
Wavelength λ = total distance ÷ 10
If the pattern moves too fast to measure, **take a photograph or video** with the ruler in the picture, then measure from the image
A **stroboscope** flashing at the same frequency as the waves makes the pattern appear **stationary**, so it can be measured easily
Convert the wavelength from cm to m before calculating speed

callouts.p: 10 wavelengths spans 11 bright lines. Divide the distance by the number of gaps between lines, not the number of lines.
