core.p: Frequency is the number of waves passing a point each second. Ripples are too fast to count one second at a time, so count over a longer time.
bullets: Choose a fixed point (a mark on the paper) and **count the number of waves passing it in 10 s**, timed with a stopwatch
Frequency f = number of waves ÷ time (for example 80 waves ÷ 10 s = 8.0 Hz)
A **video** with an on-screen timer can be slowed down to count waves more accurately
A **stroboscope**: increase its flash frequency until the pattern appears frozen; the strobe frequency then equals the wave frequency
The frequency is the same as the **vibration frequency of the bar**, which may be shown on the power supply or signal generator
Keep the motor setting constant so the frequency does not change during the experiment

callouts.p: Counting over 10 s rather than 1 s makes the error from starting and stopping the stopwatch a much smaller fraction of the time.

core.h: Calculating the speed of the ripples
core.p: Once you have the frequency and wavelength, use v = f λ. There is also a direct timing method using v = x / t.
bullets: **v = f λ**: for example f = 8.0 Hz and λ = 0.020 m gives v = 8.0 × 0.020 = **0.16 m/s**
**v = x / t**: mark two points a known distance apart (for example the length of the tank), time how long one wavefront takes to travel between them, and divide distance by time
The timing method is less accurate because the wave is hard to follow by eye and reaction time is large compared with the short time
Repeat measurements and calculate a mean speed
Both methods should give similar values if the water depth is the same

callouts.p: Ripple speeds are typically a fraction of a metre per second. If you calculate 16 m/s, check that you converted cm to m.

core.p: Grade 9 answers identify what must be kept the same and explain how each technique makes the result more accurate or more reliable.
bullets: Sound: perform outdoors on a **still day**, because wind speeds up or slows down the sound; temperature also affects the speed of sound slightly
Sound: use **large distances** for hand timing, or **electronic timing** for short distances
Sound: make **sharp, short sounds** so the start and end are clear
Ripples: keep the **water depth constant** and the tank **level**, since depth affects ripple speed
Ripples: use a **low frequency** so the waves are easy to count and the pattern is clear
Measure **many wavelengths** and **count over a long time**, then divide
**Repeat** readings and calculate a **mean**, ignoring anomalous values
Use a **camera or video** to freeze the waves and remove reaction time

callouts.t: Reaction time is a random error
callouts.p: Repeating and averaging reduces random errors such as reaction time. It does not remove a systematic error such as a wrongly measured distance.

core.p: Exam questions often ask which method is best, or why one method is more accurate than another.
bullets: Electronic timing is the most accurate for sound because there is **no reaction time**
Flash and bang is simple but needs a very large open space and still conditions
The echo method only needs one wall, but single echoes are too quick to time by hand
For ripples, v = f λ with a strobe or photograph is usually more accurate than timing one ripple

core.p: These are low-hazard experiments but method questions sometimes give a mark for a sensible safety point.
bullets: Ripple tank: **water and electricity** do not mix, so keep the power supply and plugs away from water and mop up spills straight away
Spilt water on the floor is a **slip hazard**
The lamp can get **hot**; do not touch it
A **stroboscope** flashing at certain frequencies can trigger photosensitive epilepsy, so check before using one
Starting pistols must only be used under supervision; cymbals or wooden blocks are safer alternatives

analogy.t: Timing a runner on a race track
analogy.p: Measuring the speed of sound with the flash and bang method is like timing a sprinter: the starting pistol's smoke (the flash) tells the timer to start, and the runner crossing the line (the sound arriving) tells them to stop. Distance ÷ time gives the speed. A sprinter covers 100 m in about 10 s, so a 0.2 s reaction time hardly matters, but sound covers 100 m in only 0.3 s, so the same reaction time would ruin the result; that is why sound needs a much longer track. Where it breaks down: a runner carries their own body to the finish, but a sound wave does not carry air from one person to the other; only energy moves while air particles vibrate in place.

terms.d: The distance travelled by sound each second; about 330 to 340 m/s in air.
A sound that has been reflected from a surface and is heard after the original sound.
The delay between a person seeing or hearing something and responding to it, typically about 0.2 to 0.3 s.
A wheel of known circumference that clicks each metre, used to measure long distances outdoors.
An electronic device that records readings from sensors, such as the times at which microphones detect a sound.
A device that displays a signal, such as one from a microphone, as a trace on a screen against time.
A device that produces an electrical signal of a chosen frequency to drive a loudspeaker or vibrator.
A shallow tray of water with a vibrating bar, lamp above and screen below, used to show and measure water waves.
A bar driven by a motor that dips in and out of the water to produce plane waves at a set frequency.
A lamp that flashes at an adjustable frequency; when it matches the wave frequency the waves appear stationary.
A line joining points on a wave that are at the same stage of their cycle, such as a line of crests; seen as bright lines in a ripple tank.
The total of a set of repeat readings divided by the number of readings, used to reduce the effect of random errors.
An unpredictable variation in readings, such as from reaction time, reduced by repeating and averaging.
An error that shifts every reading by the same amount or in the same direction, such as a wrongly measured distance.

mistakes.w: In the echo method, divides the distance to the wall by the time.
mistakes.r: The sound travels to the wall and back, so speed = 2 × distance to wall ÷ time.

mistakes.w: Says the flash and bang method works because light and sound start at the same time.
mistakes.r: It works because light travels so much faster than sound that the light's travel time is negligible; the measured time is the sound's travel time.

mistakes.w: Suggests standing 5 m apart and using a stopwatch to time sound.
mistakes.r: The time would be far shorter than reaction time; use a large distance (hundreds of metres) or electronic timing.

mistakes.w: Measures one wavelength of a ripple with a ruler.
mistakes.r: Measure across many wavelengths (for example 10) and divide, to reduce the percentage error.

mistakes.w: Counts 11 bright lines and divides the distance by 11.
mistakes.r: 11 lines have 10 gaps between them, so divide by 10.

mistakes.w: Says repeating the experiment makes it more accurate without explanation.
mistakes.r: Repeating and calculating a mean reduces the effect of random errors, such as reaction time, and allows anomalies to be identified.

mistakes.w: Forgets to control the water depth in a ripple tank.
mistakes.r: Keep the depth constant because the speed of ripples depends on the depth of the water.

mistakes.w: Uses a wavelength in cm with frequency in Hz to get the speed in m/s.
mistakes.r: Convert the wavelength into metres first.

exam.q: State the equation used to calculate the speed of sound from a distance and a time.
model: speed = distance ÷ time (v = x / t)
exam.tip: Words or symbols are both accepted.

exam.q: A student says she can measure the speed of sound by timing a clap over 10 m with a stopwatch. Explain why this would not give an accurate value.
model: sound takes only about 0.03 s to travel 10 m
this is much shorter than human reaction time, so the timing error is very large
exam.tip: Compare the time being measured with reaction time.

exam.q: In the flash and bang method, explain why the time taken for the light to reach the timer can be ignored.
model: light travels much faster than sound (3 × 10^8 m/s compared with about 340 m/s)
so its travel time over a few hundred metres is negligible
exam.tip: Quote both speeds for full marks.

exam.q: Two students stand 510 m apart. The time between seeing the cymbals clash and hearing the sound is 1.5 s. Calculate the speed of sound.
exam.tip: Substitute then give the unit.

exam.q: A student stands 85 m from a wall and claps in time with the echoes. 20 intervals between claps take 10.0 s. Calculate the speed of sound.
model: time for one interval = 10.0 ÷ 20 = 0.50 s
distance travelled = 2 × 85 = 170 m
exam.tip: Remember the sound goes to the wall and back.

exam.q: Give two ways to improve the accuracy of the flash and bang method.
model: increase the distance so reaction time is a smaller fraction of the measured time
repeat and calculate a mean / use several timers / swap positions to cancel wind / use a still day
exam.tip: Any two valid improvements; explaining why can earn credit in longer questions.

exam.q: In a ripple tank, a student measures the distance across 10 wavelengths as 15 cm. Explain why she measured 10 wavelengths rather than one, and calculate the wavelength in metres.
model: one wavelength is small so measuring it gives a large percentage error / measuring many reduces the uncertainty
exam.tip: Always convert to metres if the question asks.

exam.q: Describe how a stroboscope can be used to help measure the wavelength of water waves in a ripple tank.
model: adjust the strobe frequency until it equals the wave frequency so the waves appear stationary
then measure the distance across several wavefronts with a ruler and divide by the number of wavelengths
exam.tip: Say the pattern appears frozen.

exam.q: Ripples have a frequency of 6.0 Hz and a wavelength of 2.5 cm. Calculate their speed.
exam.tip: Ripple speeds are slow; 15 m/s would mean you forgot to convert.

exam.q: Explain why the depth of the water must be kept the same in a ripple tank experiment.
model: the speed of water waves depends on the depth
so changing depth would change the speed and the wavelength, making results unfair or inconsistent
exam.tip: Link depth to speed.

exam.q: Describe how to measure the speed of ripples on the surface of water in a ripple tank.
model: set up a ripple tank with water of constant depth, a vibrating bar (motor), and a lamp above shining onto paper below
switch on the motor to produce plane waves; a shadow pattern of wavefronts appears on the paper
measure the wavelength by measuring across, for example, 10 wavelengths with a ruler and dividing by 10 (or photograph the pattern with a ruler in view)
measure the frequency by counting the waves passing a point in 10 s and dividing by 10 (or using a stroboscope)
calculate speed using v = f × λ with λ in metres
repeat and calculate a mean
exam.tip: Six mark answers need a logical sequence: setup, measure λ, measure f, calculate, improve.

exam.q: Describe a method to measure the speed of sound in air using two microphones.
model: place two microphones a measured distance apart (using a metre rule) connected to a timer or datalogger
make a sharp sound in line with the microphones
the timer measures the time taken for the sound to travel from the first to the second microphone
calculate speed = distance between microphones ÷ time; repeat and average
exam.tip: State what starts and stops the timer.

worked.q: A student stands 102 m from a large wall and claps in rhythm with the echoes. Her friend times 30 intervals between claps as 18.0 s. Calculate the speed of sound.
steps: Time for one interval: t = 18.0 ÷ 30 = 0.60 s.
In each interval the sound travels to the wall and back: x = 2 × 102 = 204 m.
Equation: v = x / t.

worked.q: In a ripple tank, 11 bright lines span 20 cm, and 80 waves pass a mark in 10 s. Calculate the speed of the ripples.
steps: 11 lines means 10 wavelengths, so λ = 20 cm ÷ 10 = 2.0 cm = 0.020 m.
Frequency: f = 80 ÷ 10 = 8.0 Hz.
Equation: v = f × λ.

worked.q: A loudspeaker connected to a signal generator at 1700 Hz faces two microphones whose signals are shown on an oscilloscope. One microphone is moved away until the two traces line up again; it has moved 0.20 m. Calculate the speed of sound.
steps: When the traces line up again, the microphones are one more wavelength apart, so λ = 0.20 m.
f = 1700 Hz from the signal generator.

phy_edx.3.4.summary: This triple-only point is about using **echoes** to work out how far away something is. A pulse of sound or ultrasound is sent out, reflects off a boundary such as the seabed, a cliff or an organ inside the body, and returns; measuring the time for the round trip and knowing the wave speed lets you calculate **distance = speed × time ÷ 2**. The key grade 9 idea is that the pulse travels **there and back**, so the depth is half of the total distance travelled, and every value must be in SI units.

core.p: Edexcel spec point 4.8P (Physics only): **calculate depth or distance from time and wave velocity**. In practice this means echo calculations for **sonar (echo sounding)**, **ultrasound scanning** and echoes of sound in air.
bullets: Uses the recall equation **v = x / t**, rearranged to **x = v × t**
For an echo, the pulse travels to the object **and back**, so the distance to the object is **half** of x
**depth (or distance) d = (v × t) ÷ 2**
t is the time from sending the pulse to **receiving the echo**
v is the speed of the wave in the medium it travels through, given in the question
This point is **triple (separate) Physics only**; it can appear on Higher and Foundation papers

callouts.p: Total distance = speed × time. Depth = total distance ÷ 2, because the pulse goes there and back.

core.p: When a wave reaches a **boundary between two different materials**, some of the wave is **reflected**. A reflected sound or ultrasound wave is called an **echo**. The rest of the wave may be transmitted into the new material or absorbed.
bullets: Hard, flat surfaces such as cliffs, walls and the seabed give strong echoes
Inside the body, each **boundary between different tissues** (for example between soft tissue and bone, or the wall of an organ) reflects part of an ultrasound pulse
Because only part of the wave is reflected at each boundary, a single pulse can produce **several echoes** from boundaries at different depths
The further away the boundary, the **longer** the echo takes to return
Echoes are usually weaker than the original pulse because energy is transmitted, absorbed and spread out

callouts.p: A reflected sound (or ultrasound) wave, detected some time after the original sound was produced.

core.p: Echo distance measurement always follows the same pattern, whether it is a ship measuring the depth of the sea or a doctor scanning a fetus. A **transmitter** sends out a short **pulse**, and a **receiver** (often in the same device) detects the echo and records the time.
bullets: 1. A short pulse of sound or ultrasound is **emitted** and a timer starts
2. The pulse travels through the medium at a known speed v
3. It **reflects** at a boundary
4. The echo travels **back** to the receiver and the timer stops
5. The total distance travelled = v × t
6. The distance to the boundary = (v × t) ÷ 2
Short pulses are used so each echo can be timed separately rather than overlapping with the outgoing sound

callouts.p: In explain questions mention all four ideas: pulse sent, reflected at boundary, time for echo measured, distance = speed × time ÷ 2.

core.p: This is the single most important idea in the topic and the most common place to lose marks. The timer measures the time for the **whole journey**: from the transmitter **to** the boundary **and back** again. The depth or distance you want is only the **one-way** journey.
bullets: Total distance travelled by the pulse = 2 × depth
So depth = total distance ÷ 2 = (v × t) ÷ 2
Equivalently, you can halve the time first: one-way time = t ÷ 2, then depth = v × (t ÷ 2)
Only halve **once**: either halve the time or halve the distance, never both
If a question says the pulse is detected by a **separate receiver at the far side** (no reflection), then there is no return trip and you do **not** halve

callouts.p: Forgetting to divide by 2 gives an answer twice as big as the correct depth and usually loses the final mark.

core.p: The speed of a sound or ultrasound wave depends on the **medium** it is travelling through. Always use the speed the question gives for that medium.
bullets: Sound in air: about **340 m/s** (330 to 340 m/s)
Sound and ultrasound in sea water: about **1500 m/s**
Ultrasound in soft body tissue: about **1500 m/s** (questions may give 1540 m/s)
Sound in steel: about **5000 to 6000 m/s**
Ultrasound is a sound wave too, so it travels at the **same speed** as audible sound in the same medium
If the pulse passes through two materials, use each material's own speed for its own section of the path

head: Medium
Typical speed (m/s)
Typical echo use
rows: echo from a cliff or wall, parking sensors, bats
sonar: depth of seabed, shoals of fish, submarines
ultrasound scans of organs and fetuses

callouts.p: Underline the speed and the medium in the question. Using 340 m/s for water is a common slip.

core.h: Sonar and echo sounding at sea
core.p: Ships use **sonar** (echo sounding) to measure the depth of water beneath them. A transducer on the hull sends a pulse of sound or ultrasound downwards; the pulse reflects from the seabed and the echo is detected by the same transducer.
bullets: Depth = (speed of sound in water × echo time) ÷ 2
Example: echo time 0.80 s, speed 1500 m/s: depth = 1500 × 0.80 ÷ 2 = **600 m**
A shoal of fish or a submarine between the ship and the seabed reflects some of the pulse, giving an **earlier, extra echo**
Repeating the pulses as the ship moves builds up a **map of the seabed**
A longer echo time means **deeper** water

callouts.p: An object closer to the ship returns its echo sooner. Echo time is directly proportional to distance.

core.p: Ultrasound scans use the same pulse-echo idea. A probe placed on the skin (with gel to stop air gaps) sends pulses of ultrasound into the body. At each **boundary between different tissues**, some ultrasound is reflected and some is transmitted further in.
bullets: Each echo returns at a different time; the **time of each echo** tells the computer the **depth** of that boundary
Depth of a boundary = (speed in tissue × echo time) ÷ 2
**Thickness** of a layer = depth of far boundary − depth of near boundary
Or: thickness = (speed × difference in echo times) ÷ 2
The computer uses many echoes to build up an image, which is why ultrasound can show a fetus or an organ
Times are very short, usually in **microseconds (μs)**: 1 μs = 1 × 10^-6 s

callouts.p: Find the depth of each boundary separately, then subtract. Do not forget to halve each time.

core.h: Reading echo times from an oscilloscope
core.p: Many exam questions show the transmitted pulse and the echo as spikes on an **oscilloscope** screen. The horizontal axis is time, and the **timebase** tells you how much time each square (division) represents.
bullets: Count the number of **divisions** between the start of the transmitted pulse and the start of the echo
Echo time t = number of divisions × timebase setting (for example 5 div × 20 μs/div = 100 μs)
Convert to seconds: 100 μs = 100 × 10^-6 s = 1.0 × 10^-4 s
The echo pulse is usually **smaller** because energy is lost (partly transmitted, absorbed and spread out)
Several echo spikes mean several boundaries; each spike further to the right is a **deeper** boundary

callouts.p: The echo time is measured from the transmitted pulse to the echo, not from the left-hand edge of the screen, unless the pulse starts there.

core.p: The same calculation works for sound in air, using about 340 m/s.
bullets: Shouting at a cliff: echo after 1.2 s gives distance = 340 × 1.2 ÷ 2 = **204 m**
**Parking sensors** on cars send out ultrasound pulses and time the echoes from obstacles behind the car
**Bats** emit ultrasound and use the echo time to judge how far away insects and obstacles are (echolocation)
You can only hear a separate echo if the reflecting surface is far enough away for the echo to arrive noticeably after the original sound
You can also turn the method round: if you know the distance, the echo time gives the **speed of sound**: v = 2d ÷ t

core.p: Questions can ask for any of the three quantities. Start from 2d = v × t and rearrange.
bullets: Depth or distance: **d = (v × t) ÷ 2**
Echo time: **t = 2d ÷ v**
Wave speed: **v = 2d ÷ t**
Example: a seabed 450 m deep, speed 1500 m/s: t = 2 × 450 ÷ 1500 = **0.60 s**
Echo time is **directly proportional** to depth: twice as deep means twice the echo time

callouts.p: Writing 2d = v × t first makes every rearrangement straightforward and reminds you about the factor of 2.

core.p: Echo times are often given in milliseconds or microseconds and depths may be asked for in cm or km. Convert before calculating and check the answer is sensible.
bullets: **ms to s**: divide by 1000 (or × 10^-3)
**μs to s**: divide by 1 000 000 (or × 10^-6)
**m to cm**: multiply by 100; **m to km**: divide by 1000
A body ultrasound answer should be a few centimetres, a sea depth tens to thousands of metres, a cliff tens to hundreds of metres
Give the answer to a sensible number of significant figures (usually matching the data)

callouts.p: If an ultrasound depth comes out as 75 m, you have forgotten to convert microseconds into seconds.

core.p: Higher-level questions may ask why echo measurements might not be exactly right, or how they could be improved.
bullets: The speed of sound in sea water varies slightly with **temperature** and **salt content**, so the depth calculated using an average speed is approximate
Soft tissues have slightly different speeds; machines assume one average value
A soft or uneven seabed may **absorb** or **scatter** the pulse, giving a weak or unclear echo
An object between the transmitter and the target (fish, bubbles) may give a false, earlier echo
Using **electronic timing** gives much more accurate times than any manual method
Taking **repeat readings** and calculating a mean reduces random error

analogy.t: Throwing a tennis ball at a wall
analogy.p: Imagine throwing a tennis ball at a wall at a steady speed and timing how long it takes to bounce back to your hand. The ball travels to the wall and back, so to find how far away the wall is you must halve the total distance: exactly like an echo. Throw it twice as far and it takes twice as long to come back, just as a deeper seabed gives a longer echo time. Where it breaks down: the ball itself travels to the wall and back, but in a sound echo no air travels from you to the wall; only energy is carried by vibrating particles. Also, a wave partly reflects and partly passes through a boundary, giving several echoes, while a ball simply bounces.

terms.d: A reflected sound or ultrasound wave, detected after the original sound.
A short burst of waves sent out so that its echo can be timed.
Sending a pulse, timing how long the echo takes to return, and using distance = speed × time ÷ 2.
Using pulses of sound or ultrasound and their echoes to find the depth of water or the position of underwater objects.
Sound with a frequency higher than 20 000 Hz, above the range of human hearing.
A device that both sends out the pulse and detects the returning echo, such as an ultrasound probe.
The surface where two different materials meet; part of a wave is reflected there.
The time between sending a pulse and receiving its echo; the time for the there-and-back journey.
The one-way distance from the transmitter to the reflecting boundary, d = (v × t) ÷ 2.
The distance a wave travels per second in a particular medium, in m/s.
A device that displays signals against time, used to show the transmitted pulse and its echoes.
The oscilloscope setting giving the time represented by each horizontal division, for example 20 μs per division.
One millionth of a second, 1 × 10^-6 s.
The use of ultrasound echoes by animals such as bats and dolphins to find the distance to objects.

mistakes.w: Depth = speed × time (forgets to halve).
mistakes.r: Depth = (speed × time) ÷ 2, because the pulse travels to the boundary and back.

mistakes.w: Halves the time and then halves the distance as well.
mistakes.r: Halve only once: either use half the echo time or halve the total distance.

mistakes.w: Uses 340 m/s for a pulse travelling through sea water or body tissue.
mistakes.r: Use the speed for that medium given in the question, such as 1500 m/s in water or tissue.

mistakes.w: Uses an echo time in μs or ms without converting.
mistakes.r: Convert to seconds first: μs × 10^-6, ms × 10^-3.

mistakes.w: Says ultrasound travels faster than audible sound.
mistakes.r: Ultrasound is sound; in the same medium it travels at the same speed as audible sound.

mistakes.w: Finds the thickness of a layer using only the later echo time.
mistakes.r: Thickness = depth of far boundary − depth of near boundary, or speed × difference in echo times ÷ 2.

mistakes.w: Reads the echo time from the left edge of the oscilloscope screen.
mistakes.r: Measure the time between the transmitted pulse and the echo pulse, using divisions × timebase.

mistakes.w: Says all of the pulse is reflected at a boundary.
mistakes.r: Only part of the wave is reflected; the rest is transmitted or absorbed, which is why several echoes are received.

mistakes.w: Rearranges to t = d ÷ v for an echo.
mistakes.r: Echo time t = 2d ÷ v.

exam.q: State what is meant by an echo.
model: a reflected sound (wave)
exam.tip: Use the word reflected.

exam.q: Explain why the depth of the sea is found by halving the distance calculated from speed × echo time.
model: the pulse travels from the ship to the seabed and back again
so the total distance is twice the depth
exam.tip: Say there and back.

exam.q: A ship sends a sound pulse to the seabed. The echo is received 0.80 s later. The speed of sound in sea water is 1500 m/s. Calculate the depth of the sea.
model: distance travelled = 1500 × 0.80 = 1200 m
depth = 1200 ÷ 2
exam.tip: Show the halving step clearly.

exam.q: A student shouts towards a cliff and hears the echo 1.2 s later. The speed of sound in air is 340 m/s. Calculate the distance to the cliff.
model: total distance = 340 × 1.2 = 408 m
distance to cliff = 408 ÷ 2
exam.tip: Same method in air, different speed.

exam.q: The seabed is 900 m below a ship. The speed of sound in sea water is 1500 m/s. Calculate the time between sending a pulse and receiving its echo.
model: total distance = 2 × 900 = 1800 m
exam.tip: Double the depth before dividing by speed.

exam.q: On an oscilloscope, an echo is 4 divisions after the transmitted pulse. The timebase is 50 μs per division. Calculate the echo time in seconds.
exam.tip: Count divisions between the two pulses, then convert.

exam.q: Using your answer to the previous question, calculate the depth of the boundary in the body. Ultrasound travels at 1500 m/s in tissue.
model: distance travelled = 1500 × 2.0 × 10^-4 = 0.30 m
depth = 0.30 ÷ 2
exam.tip: Body depths are a few cm to tens of cm.

exam.q: A fishing boat's sonar receives two echoes from one pulse: one after 0.20 s and one after 0.50 s. Explain what each echo is likely to come from.
model: the earlier echo (0.20 s) is from an object closer to the boat, such as a shoal of fish
the later echo (0.50 s) is from the seabed, which is further away
exam.tip: Earlier echo means nearer object.

exam.q: An ultrasound pulse produces echoes from the front and back of an organ at 40 μs and 70 μs. The speed of ultrasound in tissue is 1500 m/s. Calculate the thickness of the organ.
model: thickness = 0.0525 − 0.030
exam.tip: Or use the time difference: 1500 × 30 × 10^-6 ÷ 2.

exam.q: Suggest why the depth of the sea measured by sonar may not be exactly correct.
model: the speed of sound in sea water varies with temperature / salinity / depth
so the value of speed used may not be the actual speed (or: an uneven seabed scatters the pulse, giving an unclear echo)
exam.tip: Link the reason to the value used in the calculation.

exam.q: Describe how a ship uses sonar to measure the depth of water beneath it, and explain how the depth is calculated.
model: a transmitter on the ship sends a short pulse of sound / ultrasound downwards
the pulse travels through the water at a known speed (about 1500 m/s)
it is reflected by the seabed (boundary)
the echo is detected by a receiver on the ship and the time from sending to receiving is measured
total distance travelled = speed × time
depth = total distance ÷ 2 because the pulse travels to the seabed and back
exam.tip: Six mark answers need the full sequence and the reason for halving.

worked.q: A ship's sonar pulse returns from the seabed after 2.4 s. Sound travels at 1500 m/s in sea water. Calculate the depth of the water in km.
steps: Total distance: x = v × t = 1500 × 2.4 = 3600 m.
The pulse went down and back up, so depth d = 3600 ÷ 2 = 1800 m.
Convert: 1800 m ÷ 1000 = 1.8 km.
worked.ans: Depth = 1800 m = 1.8 km

worked.q: An oscilloscope shows an ultrasound echo 5 divisions after the transmitted pulse. The timebase is 20 μs per division and ultrasound travels at 1500 m/s in tissue. Calculate the depth of the boundary in cm.
steps: Echo time: t = 5 × 20 μs = 100 μs = 1.0 × 10^-4 s.
Total distance: x = 1500 × 1.0 × 10^-4 = 0.15 m.
worked.ans: Depth = 7.5 cm

worked.q: Ultrasound echoes from the near and far sides of a layer of tissue arrive 40 μs and 70 μs after the pulse is sent. The speed of ultrasound in tissue is 1500 m/s. Calculate the thickness of the layer.
steps: Difference in echo times = 70 − 40 = 30 μs = 3.0 × 10^-5 s.
Extra distance travelled (there and back across the layer) = 1500 × 3.0 × 10^-5 = 0.045 m.
Check: depths are 0.030 m and 0.0525 m, difference 0.0225 m.
worked.ans: Thickness = 0.0225 m (about 2.3 cm)

phy_edx.3.5.summary: When a wave reaches the **boundary between two different materials**, its energy can be **reflected** (bounced back), **refracted** (changes speed and usually direction), **transmitted** (passes through) or **absorbed** (energy transferred to the material, usually heating it). In real situations a mixture of these happens at once, and the share of each depends on the two materials and on the wavelength of the wave. Because energy is conserved, the energy arriving always equals the energy reflected plus transmitted plus absorbed.

core.h: What can happen at a boundary
core.p: A **boundary** (or interface) is where one material meets another, such as air and glass, air and water, or muscle and bone. When a wave arrives at a boundary it carries energy with it, and that energy has to go somewhere. Edexcel expects you to describe four effects: reflection, refraction, transmission and absorption.
bullets: **Reflection**: the wave bounces back into the first material.
**Refraction**: the wave enters the second material and changes speed, which usually changes its direction.
**Transmission**: the wave carries on through the second material and comes out the other side.
**Absorption**: the wave's energy is transferred to the particles of the material, usually increasing its **thermal energy store** (it warms up).
These are **not either-or**: most boundaries reflect some energy, absorb some and transmit some.
Which effect dominates depends on the **materials** on each side and on the **wavelength (frequency)** of the wave.

callouts.p: A wave at a boundary is split up: part reflected, part transmitted (often refracted), and part absorbed. The total energy is unchanged.

core.p: **Reflection** happens when a wave hits a boundary and bounces back into the material it came from. It happens with all types of wave: light from a mirror, sound as an echo, water waves from a harbour wall, and ultrasound from the boundary between two body tissues.
bullets: The reflected wave stays in the **same material**, so its **speed, frequency and wavelength are unchanged**.
Smooth, hard, flat surfaces are **good reflectors** (mirrors for light, hard walls for sound).
Reflection of sound gives an **echo**; reflection of light lets us see objects that do not give out their own light.
The bigger the difference between the two materials, the more of the wave tends to be reflected (for example, ultrasound reflects strongly at a tissue and bone or tissue and air boundary).
Some energy is usually lost to absorption even at a good reflector, so the reflected wave has a **smaller amplitude** than the incident wave.

callouts.p: Reflection is when a wave bounces off a boundary between two materials and returns into the first material.

core.h: The law of reflection and the normal
core.p: To describe directions at a boundary we draw a **normal**: a construction line at **90 degrees to the surface** at the point where the wave hits. All angles are measured between the ray and the normal, never between the ray and the surface.
bullets: **Angle of incidence (i)**: angle between the incident ray and the normal.
**Angle of reflection (r)**: angle between the reflected ray and the normal.
**Law of reflection: angle of incidence = angle of reflection.**
The incident ray, reflected ray and normal all lie in the **same plane**.
A ray that hits along the normal (i = 0) reflects straight back along itself.
Draw the normal as a **dashed line** and put arrows on rays to show the direction of travel.

callouts.p: If a question says a ray hits a mirror at 30 degrees to the surface, the angle of incidence is 90 - 30 = 60 degrees.

core.p: How a surface reflects depends on how smooth it is compared with the wavelength. A very smooth surface reflects every part of a beam in the same direction; a rough surface has normals pointing in many directions, so the reflected rays scatter.
bullets: **Specular reflection**: from a smooth surface, parallel rays stay parallel, so you see a clear image (a mirror or still water).
**Diffuse (scattered) reflection**: from a rough surface, each ray still obeys i = r but the normals point different ways, so the light is scattered and no clear image forms (paper, a wall).
Sound reflects well from **hard, smooth** surfaces such as tiled walls, which is why empty halls echo.
**Soft, uneven** materials such as curtains, carpets and foam break up and absorb sound, reducing echoes.
Water waves reflect from a flat barrier in a ripple tank with the same angle rule.

callouts.t: Rough does not break the law
callouts.p: In diffuse reflection the law of reflection still applies to every individual ray; it is the surface normals that vary.

core.p: When a wave crosses a boundary into a material where it travels at a **different speed**, it is **refracted**. If it arrives at an angle to the normal, the change in speed makes it **change direction**. This point links to the core spec points on refraction, but at the triple level you must describe it as one of the four boundary effects.
bullets: Entering a material where it travels **slower** (e.g. air into glass), the wave bends **towards the normal**.
Entering a material where it travels **faster** (e.g. glass into air), the wave bends **away from the normal**.
Travelling **along the normal** (i = 0), the speed changes but the direction does **not**.
The **frequency does not change** at a boundary, so if speed falls the **wavelength gets shorter** (v = f x wavelength).
Some of the wave is usually reflected at the same time as the rest is refracted, which is why you can see a faint reflection in a window.

callouts.p: Refraction is caused by the change in wave speed when the wave enters a different material.

core.p: **Transmission** means the wave passes through a material and continues out the other side. A material that transmits a wave well is said to be **transparent** to that wave. Transmission and refraction often happen together: the wave is transmitted into the new material and refracted at the boundary.
bullets: Glass and clear water **transmit** visible light; that is why you can see through them.
Air transmits sound; walls transmit some sound (you can hear next door's music, quietly).
Radio waves are transmitted through walls, which is why a radio works indoors.
Soft body tissue transmits X-rays, while bone absorbs much more of them.
A transmitted wave keeps the **same frequency**, but its **amplitude usually falls** because some energy is absorbed on the way through.
Translucent materials transmit light but scatter it, so you cannot see a clear image through them.

callouts.p: Transmission is when a wave passes through a material and out the other side.

core.p: **Absorption** means the wave's energy is transferred to the particles of the material, so the wave gets weaker and may stop completely. The absorbed energy usually ends up in the material's **thermal energy store**, so the material warms up. A material that absorbs all of a wave is **opaque** to it.
bullets: Dark, matt surfaces **absorb** most visible light and infrared, so they heat up in sunshine.
Water molecules in food **absorb microwaves**, which heats the food in a microwave oven.
Soft furnishings, foam and carpets **absorb sound**, so rooms with them sound less echoey.
Bone **absorbs X-rays** more than soft tissue, which is why bones show up on an X-ray image.
The thicker the absorbing material, the more energy it absorbs and the less is transmitted.
Absorption can be useful (cooking, solar heating, soundproofing) or a problem (signal loss, damage to living cells by ionising radiation).

callouts.p: Absorption is when the energy of a wave is transferred to the material it meets, usually increasing the material's thermal energy store.

callouts.t: Do not say the wave is destroyed
callouts.p: The energy is not lost; it is transferred to the material. Say 'energy is transferred to the thermal store of the material'.

core.p: Because energy cannot be created or destroyed, the energy carried by the incident wave must be shared out between the reflected, transmitted and absorbed parts. This is very useful in calculations and in explaining why each part is weaker than the original.
bullets: **Incident energy = reflected energy + transmitted energy + absorbed energy.**
If more is reflected, less is left to be transmitted or absorbed.
A good mirror reflects most light; a black surface absorbs most; clear glass transmits most.
The reflected and transmitted waves both have **smaller amplitudes** than the incident wave.
In a sound-proofed room, sound energy is mainly absorbed by the walls rather than reflected or transmitted.

callouts.p: E incident = E reflected + E transmitted + E absorbed

core.h: It depends on the material and the wavelength
core.p: The same material can behave completely differently for different waves. What happens depends on the **type of material**, the **surface**, the **thickness**, and the **wavelength (or frequency)** of the wave.
bullets: Glass **transmits visible light** but **absorbs** much **ultraviolet** and some infrared.
The Earth's atmosphere transmits visible light and radio waves, but the **ozone layer absorbs** much UV.
Skin and flesh **transmit X-rays** but **absorb** most visible light.
Water strongly **absorbs microwaves** of the wavelength used in microwave ovens.
Low-frequency (long wavelength) sound passes through walls more easily than high-frequency sound, which is why you mainly hear the bass from next door.
The angle of incidence also matters: more light is reflected from water at a glancing angle.

callouts.t: Name the material and the wave
callouts.p: Six-mark answers score well when each effect is paired with a specific material and a specific wave, for example 'glass transmits visible light'.

core.h: What changes and what stays the same
core.p: Students lose marks by mixing up which quantities change at a boundary. The **frequency is set by the source**, so it never changes when a wave crosses into a new material or reflects.
bullets: **Reflection**: speed, frequency and wavelength all **unchanged**; direction reverses (obeying i = r); amplitude may fall.
**Refraction / transmission**: **frequency unchanged**; speed changes; wavelength changes in the same proportion as speed; direction changes unless along the normal.
**Absorption**: amplitude (and energy) of the wave decreases; the material's thermal store increases.
For any wave, v = f x wavelength, so with f fixed, wavelength is proportional to speed.

callouts.p: Never write that frequency changes when a wave enters a new material. Only speed and wavelength change.

core.p: Many technologies rely on choosing materials that reflect, transmit or absorb particular waves. In explain questions, link the effect to why it is useful.
bullets: **Echo sounding and sonar**: sound or ultrasound reflects from the sea bed or fish.
**Ultrasound scans**: partial reflection at each boundary between tissues builds an image, while the rest of the pulse is transmitted deeper.
**Microwave oven**: metal case and mesh reflect microwaves to keep them inside; food absorbs them; glass and plastic containers transmit them.
**Soundproofing**: soft, porous materials absorb sound rather than reflect or transmit it.
**Windows**: glass transmits light so we can see out, but some light is always reflected.
**X-ray imaging**: bone absorbs X-rays, soft tissue transmits them, creating a shadow picture.

callouts.p: Do not just name the use. Say which effect happens, in which material, and why that helps.

core.p: Questions on this point are often describe or explain questions, sometimes with a diagram to complete. Precise words and careful ray diagrams earn the marks.
bullets: Use the exact words **reflected, refracted, transmitted, absorbed**.
On diagrams, draw a **normal** with a ruler at 90 degrees to the surface, and add **arrows** to every ray.
When completing a reflection, make the reflected angle **equal** to the incident angle by measuring with a protractor.
For absorption, always say where the energy goes: the **thermal energy store** of the material.
In 6-mark questions, cover more than one effect and give an example for each.
Remember that boundary effects usually happen **together**, so answers like 'some is reflected and some is transmitted' are often expected.

callouts.p: Describe = say what happens. Explain = say what happens and why (link to speed change, energy transfer or surface type).

analogy.t: A crowd at a stadium gate
analogy.p: Imagine a crowd of people (the wave's energy) arriving at a gate (the boundary). Some people bounce off the barrier and head back (reflection), some go through the gate and carry on into the stadium (transmission), and some get tired and stop to sit down at the gate (absorption, energy handed to the material). If the ground on the other side is muddy, the people who get through slow down and, if they arrive at an angle, swing round (refraction). The total number of people never changes, just as the total energy is conserved. Where it breaks down: a real wave is not made of separate people, and every part of a wave can be partly reflected and partly transmitted at the same time, rather than each bit choosing one route.

terms.d: The surface where two different materials meet.
When a wave bounces off a boundary and returns into the first material.
The change in direction of a wave crossing a boundary at an angle, caused by a change in its speed.
When a wave passes through a material and out the other side.
When the energy of a wave is transferred to the material it meets, usually to its thermal energy store.
A construction line drawn at 90 degrees to a surface at the point where a wave or ray meets it.
The angle between the incident ray and the normal.
The angle between the reflected ray and the normal.
The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection.
Reflection from a smooth surface in which parallel rays stay parallel, producing a clear image.
Reflection from a rough surface in which rays are scattered in many directions.
Describes a material that transmits a particular wave with little scattering, so a clear image can be seen through it.
Describes a material that transmits light but scatters it, so no clear image is seen.
Describes a material that does not transmit a particular wave; it reflects or absorbs it.
A reflected sound wave heard after the original sound.
The energy store that increases when a material absorbs a wave and its temperature rises.

mistakes.w: The angle of incidence is the angle between the ray and the mirror.
mistakes.r: Angles are measured between the ray and the normal, at 90 degrees to the surface.

mistakes.w: The frequency of the wave changes when it goes into glass.
mistakes.r: Frequency stays the same; the speed and wavelength change.

mistakes.w: When a wave is absorbed the energy disappears.
mistakes.r: The energy is transferred to the material, usually increasing its thermal energy store.

mistakes.w: A wave is either reflected or transmitted.
mistakes.r: At most boundaries some of the wave is reflected, some transmitted and some absorbed at the same time.

mistakes.w: Refraction is when a wave bends.
mistakes.r: Refraction is a change in direction caused by a change in speed as the wave enters a different material.

mistakes.w: A rough surface does not obey the law of reflection.
mistakes.r: Every ray still obeys angle of incidence = angle of reflection; the normals point in different directions, so the light is scattered.

mistakes.w: A wave travelling along the normal bends.
mistakes.r: Along the normal the speed and wavelength change but the direction does not.

mistakes.w: Reflected waves travel faster or slower than the incident wave.
mistakes.r: The reflected wave stays in the same material, so its speed, frequency and wavelength are unchanged.

exam.q: State what is meant by the absorption of a wave.
model: The energy of the wave is transferred to the material (increasing its thermal energy store).
exam.tip: Mention energy transfer to the material, not just 'the wave stops'.

exam.q: A ray of light hits a plane mirror. The angle between the ray and the mirror surface is 25 degrees. State the angle of reflection.
model: 65 degrees.
exam.tip: Convert to the angle from the normal first: 90 - 25.

exam.q: Name the effect that happens when sound bounces off a cliff, and state what we hear as a result.
model: Reflection.
An echo.
exam.tip: Two separate facts, two marks.

exam.q: Complete the ray diagram to show light reflecting from a mirror. Label the angle of incidence and the angle of reflection.
model: Normal drawn at 90 degrees to the mirror at the point of incidence.
Reflected ray drawn with angle of reflection equal to angle of incidence (by eye or protractor) and an arrow.
Both angles correctly labelled between the rays and the normal.
exam.tip: Use a ruler and protractor; arrows on rays are often required.

exam.q: Explain why a room with carpets and curtains sounds much less echoey than an empty room with bare walls.
model: Hard, smooth walls reflect most sound, producing echoes.
Soft materials absorb sound energy, so less is reflected.
exam.tip: Contrast reflection and absorption clearly.

exam.q: Light travels from air into a glass block at an angle. Describe what happens to the speed, frequency, wavelength and direction of the light.
model: Speed decreases.
Frequency stays the same.
Wavelength decreases.
Direction changes: it bends towards the normal.
exam.tip: One mark per quantity: list them in order.

exam.q: A beam of microwaves carrying 800 J of energy hits a food container. 120 J is reflected and 500 J is transmitted. Calculate the energy absorbed.
model: Absorbed = 800 - 120 - 500
exam.tip: Use incident = reflected + transmitted + absorbed.

exam.q: Explain why a black car gets hotter in sunlight than a silver car.
model: The black surface absorbs more of the light and infrared.
The silver surface reflects more of it.
Absorbed energy is transferred to the car's thermal energy store, so its temperature rises more.
exam.tip: Link absorption to the thermal store and temperature.

exam.q: Explain why you can see a faint reflection of yourself in a shop window while also seeing the goods inside.
model: Most of the light is transmitted through the glass so you see inside.
A small amount of light is reflected at the boundary, forming a faint image.
exam.tip: Show that both effects happen at the same time.

exam.q: Describe how different materials are used in a microwave oven in terms of reflection, transmission and absorption of microwaves.
model: The metal walls and the metal mesh in the door reflect microwaves.
This keeps the microwaves inside the oven (and away from the user).
Glass or plastic containers transmit microwaves.
Water in the food absorbs microwaves, so energy is transferred to the food's thermal store and it heats up.
exam.tip: Give a material and an effect for each part.

exam.q: Discuss what can happen to waves when they meet a boundary between two materials. Use examples of different waves in your answer.
model: Waves can be reflected: they bounce back into the first material, e.g. light from a mirror or sound as an echo.
Angle of incidence equals angle of reflection, measured from the normal.
Waves can be transmitted: they pass through, e.g. light through glass or X-rays through soft tissue.
Waves can be refracted: they change speed on entering a new material and change direction if at an angle, e.g. light into glass bends towards the normal.
Waves can be absorbed: energy is transferred to the material's thermal store, e.g. microwaves absorbed by water, X-rays by bone.
Usually a combination happens; what happens depends on the material and the wavelength, and frequency is unchanged.
exam.tip: Level-marked: cover all four effects, each with an example, and add the wavelength dependence for top marks.

worked.q: A sound wave carrying 50 J of energy hits a wall. 60% of the energy is reflected and 15 J is transmitted into the next room. How much energy is absorbed by the wall, and where does it go?
steps: Reflected energy = 60% of 50 J = 0.60 x 50 = 30 J.
Use energy conservation: incident = reflected + transmitted + absorbed.
Absorbed = 50 - 30 - 15 = 5 J.
The absorbed energy is transferred to the wall's thermal energy store (the wall warms very slightly).
worked.ans: 5 J absorbed, transferred to the thermal energy store of the wall.

worked.q: A ray of light strikes a mirror at an angle of 38 degrees to the mirror surface. Find the angle of incidence, the angle of reflection, and the angle between the incident and reflected rays.
steps: Angle of incidence is measured from the normal: 90 - 38 = 52 degrees.
Law of reflection: angle of reflection = angle of incidence = 52 degrees.
Angle between the two rays = 52 + 52 = 104 degrees.
worked.ans: i = 52 degrees, r = 52 degrees, angle between rays = 104 degrees.

worked.q: A student shines a lamp at a sheet of clear glass, a sheet of white paper and a sheet of black card. Describe what happens to the light at each.
steps: Clear glass: most light is transmitted (refracted at each surface), a little is reflected, very little absorbed.
White paper: most light is reflected diffusely (scattered) because the surface is rough; some is transmitted (it is translucent); little absorbed.
Black card: most light is absorbed, transferring energy to the card's thermal store, so it warms up; very little is reflected.
worked.ans: Glass mainly transmits, white paper mainly diffusely reflects, black card mainly absorbs.

phy_edx.3.6.summary: **Refraction** happens because a wave **changes speed** when it crosses a boundary into a different material; if it meets the boundary at an angle, one side of each wavefront changes speed first, so the wave **changes direction**. Slowing down bends a wave **towards the normal**, speeding up bends it **away from the normal**, and along the normal there is no change of direction. The **frequency never changes**, so the wavelength changes in proportion to the speed. Different substances absorb, transmit, refract or reflect waves differently depending on **wavelength**, which explains effects such as glass transmitting light but absorbing UV, and prisms splitting white light.

core.p: **Refraction** is the change in direction of a wave when it passes from one material (medium) into another at an angle. The direction change is not the cause; it is the result. The cause is the **change in speed** of the wave in the new material.
bullets: Waves travel at different speeds in different materials.
Light is **slower in glass and water** than in air.
Water waves are **slower in shallow water** than in deep water (seen in a ripple tank).
Sound travels **faster in solids and liquids** than in air.
If the wave crosses the boundary **at an angle**, the speed change makes it change direction.
If it crosses **along the normal**, it changes speed but **keeps the same direction**.

callouts.p: Refraction is the change in direction of a wave at a boundary between two materials, caused by a change in the speed of the wave.

core.p: We describe refraction using the **normal**, a construction line at **90 degrees** to the boundary at the point where the ray crosses it. The angles are always measured from the normal.
bullets: **Angle of incidence (i)**: between the incident ray and the normal.
**Angle of refraction (r)**: between the refracted ray and the normal.
Slower in the second material: r is **smaller** than i (bends towards the normal).
Faster in the second material: r is **larger** than i (bends away from the normal).
Draw the normal as a dashed line with a ruler and put arrows on rays.

callouts.p: Angles measured from the boundary surface get no marks. Always measure from the normal.

core.h: Towards or away from the normal
core.p: The rule to learn is simple and works for every type of wave. It is about **speed**, not 'density', although for light, optically denser materials are the ones where light travels more slowly.
bullets: **Faster to slower** medium: bends **towards** the normal (e.g. light from air into glass, water waves from deep to shallow).
**Slower to faster** medium: bends **away from** the normal (e.g. light from glass into air, water into air).
**Along the normal**: no bending, but speed and wavelength still change.
The bigger the change in speed, the more the wave bends.

callouts.p: Slower = towards the normal. Faster = away from the normal.

core.h: Why speed change causes a change in direction
core.p: Think of a **wavefront** (a line joining points on the wave that are in step, such as all the crests). When a wavefront meets a boundary at an angle, **one end reaches the new material first**. That end slows down while the rest of the wavefront is still travelling at the old, faster speed. The fast part catches up on the slow part, so the wavefront **pivots** and the direction of travel changes.
bullets: The part of the wavefront in the slower material covers **less distance** in the same time.
So the wavefronts in the slower material are **closer together** (shorter wavelength).
The wavefronts become **more parallel to the boundary**, so the direction of travel turns **towards the normal**.
The reverse happens when the wave speeds up: the wavefront swings the other way and bends away from the normal.
If the wavefront arrives **parallel to the boundary** (travelling along the normal), every part slows down at the same moment, so there is nothing to make it turn.

callouts.p: For full marks say: one side of the wavefront enters the new medium first and changes speed, while the other side is still at the original speed, so the wavefront changes direction.

fig.cap: Wavefronts crossing from air into glass at an angle. The left end of each wavefront enters the glass first and slows down, so the wavefronts get closer together and pivot, turning the direction of travel towards the normal.

core.h: Frequency stays the same, wavelength changes
core.p: The **frequency of a wave is set by its source** and does not change when the wave crosses a boundary: the same number of waves per second must arrive at and leave the boundary, or waves would pile up or disappear there. Using **wave speed = frequency x wavelength (v = f x wavelength)**, if f is fixed then wavelength must change in proportion to speed.
bullets: Speed **decreases** so wavelength **decreases** (wavefronts bunch up).
Speed **increases** so wavelength **increases** (wavefronts spread out).
Wavelength is **directly proportional** to speed when frequency is constant.
For light, a change in frequency would mean a change in colour, and light does not change colour going into a glass block.
The amplitude may also decrease because some energy is reflected or absorbed at the boundary.

callouts.p: At a boundary: frequency constant; speed and wavelength change together (v = f x wavelength).

fig.cap: A wave arriving along the normal (at 90 degrees to the boundary). It slows down in the glass and its wavelength shortens, but its direction does not change.

core.h: Light through a rectangular glass block
core.p: A ray entering a rectangular glass block at an angle refracts **twice**: towards the normal as it enters (slows down) and away from the normal as it leaves (speeds up). Because the two faces are parallel, the **emergent ray is parallel to the incident ray** but shifted sideways.
bullets: At the first face: air to glass, speed decreases, bends **towards the normal**.
Inside the block: the ray travels in a straight line.
At the second face: glass to air, speed increases, bends **away from the normal**.
Emergent ray is **parallel** to the incident ray (laterally displaced).
A ray entering along the normal goes straight through without bending.
Some light is reflected at each surface too.

callouts.p: Draw a separate normal at each face where the ray crosses, and check your emergent ray is parallel to the incoming one.

core.h: Refraction of water waves in a ripple tank
core.p: Water waves travel more slowly in **shallow water** because of friction with the bottom. In a ripple tank, a glass or plastic plate placed under the water makes a shallow region, so you can watch refraction directly.
bullets: Over the shallow region the waves **slow down**, and the wavefronts are **closer together** (shorter wavelength).
If the wavefronts meet the edge of the shallow region at an angle, they **change direction** towards the normal.
The frequency is unchanged because it is set by the vibrating dipper (the source).
Waves approaching a beach slow down in shallower water and swing round, so they tend to arrive roughly parallel to the shore.

callouts.p: Deep to shallow: slower, shorter wavelength, bends towards the normal.

core.p: Refraction is not just a light effect. Any wave that changes speed at a boundary refracts. Sound travels faster in water and solids than in air, so sound entering water from air speeds up.
bullets: Sound in air is about 330 to 340 m/s; in water about 1500 m/s; in steel about 5000 m/s or more.
Sound passing from air into water at an angle **speeds up** and bends **away from the normal**.
Frequency stays the same, so its wavelength in water is **longer** than in air.
Notice this is opposite to light, which slows down in water.

callouts.p: Sound is faster in denser solids, light is slower in denser glass. Always reason from the speed change, not from density.

core.h: Responses of substances depend on wavelength
core.p: Spec point 4.11 says that **different substances may absorb, transmit, refract or reflect waves in ways that vary with wavelength**. The same material can be transparent to one wavelength and opaque to another. This is why we choose different materials for different jobs.
bullets: **Glass** transmits visible light but absorbs much **ultraviolet** (and some infrared).
The **ozone layer** in the atmosphere absorbs much of the Sun's ultraviolet.
**Soft tissue** transmits X-rays, but **bone** absorbs them more strongly.
**Water** absorbs microwaves of the wavelength used in microwave ovens, heating food.
Some long-wavelength **radio waves** are reflected by the ionosphere, while **microwaves** pass through the atmosphere to and from satellites.
**Coloured filters** transmit some wavelengths of visible light and absorb others: a red filter transmits red and absorbs other colours.
Coloured objects **reflect** some wavelengths of light and absorb the rest: a green leaf reflects mostly green.

callouts.p: How a material responds to a wave depends on the wavelength. A material can transmit one wavelength and absorb another.

core.h: Refraction also depends on wavelength: dispersion
core.p: In glass, the speed of light depends slightly on its wavelength. **Shorter wavelengths (violet, blue) travel a little more slowly** in glass than longer wavelengths (red), so they are refracted more. A triangular prism therefore splits white light into a spectrum. This is called **dispersion** and is a clear example of a substance refracting waves in a way that varies with wavelength.
bullets: White light is a mixture of wavelengths.
**Violet is refracted most, red least.**
The spectrum order is red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet.
A rectangular block barely shows dispersion because the second face undoes the first; a prism's angled faces add the bending together.
Rainbows form because water droplets refract (and reflect) different wavelengths by different amounts.

callouts.p: Different wavelengths, different speeds in glass, different amounts of refraction, so colours separate.

core.p: Refraction has everyday consequences that exam questions like to ask about, usually expecting you to name the speed change and the bending direction.
bullets: A pool looks **shallower** than it is because light from the bottom speeds up leaving the water and bends away from the normal.
A straw in water looks **bent** at the surface for the same reason.
**Lenses** in glasses, cameras and eyes use refraction to focus light.
Ocean waves refract in shallow water, so they bend round to meet the beach almost head on.
Ultrasound and seismic waves refract inside the body and the Earth when their speed changes.

core.p: Refraction questions reward precise cause-and-effect language and accurate diagrams. Always start your explanation with the speed change.
bullets: Say: the wave **changes speed** when it enters the new medium; because it is at an angle, it **changes direction**.
State which way: **towards** the normal if it slows down, **away** if it speeds up.
Always say the **frequency stays the same**, and the wavelength changes.
In v = f x wavelength calculations, use the same frequency on both sides of the boundary.
For 4.11 questions, pair a specific substance with a specific wavelength and a specific response.

callouts.p: Writing 'the wave bends because it goes into a denser material' gets little credit. Write 'it slows down'.

analogy.t: A marching band walking onto mud
analogy.p: Picture a line of marchers (a wavefront) walking at an angle from a smooth road onto a muddy field. The marchers at one end reach the mud first and slow down, while those still on the road keep their pace. The line swings round, changing the direction the band is marching, towards the normal. The band keeps the same drum beat (frequency), but on the mud each step is shorter, so the rows get closer together (shorter wavelength). If the band walks straight onto the mud, all the marchers slow at once and the direction does not change. Where it breaks down: marchers choose to slow down, but a wave's speed is set by the medium; and real waves can also be partly reflected at the edge of the mud.

mistakes.r: Refraction is a change in direction caused by a change in speed at a boundary.

mistakes.r: Frequency stays the same; speed and wavelength decrease.

mistakes.w: Light bends away from the normal when it enters glass.
mistakes.r: Light slows down entering glass so it bends towards the normal.

mistakes.w: A ray along the normal is not refracted, so nothing changes.
mistakes.r: Its direction does not change, but its speed and wavelength still change.

mistakes.r: The wave bends because its speed changes in the new material.

mistakes.r: Angles of incidence and refraction are measured from the normal.

mistakes.r: Violet (shorter wavelength) slows more in glass so it is refracted most.

exam.q: State what causes refraction.
model: A change in the speed of the wave when it enters a different medium.
exam.tip: Speed change is the key phrase.

exam.q: State which property of a wave does not change when it is refracted.
model: Frequency.
exam.tip: Not speed, not wavelength.

exam.q: Light travels from glass into air at an angle. State and explain the change in direction.
model: It bends away from the normal.
Because it speeds up when it enters the air.
exam.tip: Direction plus reason.

exam.q: Complete the diagram to show a ray of light passing through a rectangular glass block and out the other side.
model: Ray bends towards the normal on entering the block.
Ray bends away from the normal on leaving.
Emergent ray parallel to incident ray.
exam.tip: Draw normals at both faces.

exam.q: Water waves travel from deep water into shallow water. Their speed changes from 0.30 m/s to 0.18 m/s. The frequency is 1.5 Hz. Calculate the wavelength in the shallow water.
model: wavelength = v / f = 0.18 / 1.5
exam.tip: Frequency is the same in both regions.

exam.q: Explain why a wave travelling along the normal to a boundary does not change direction even though it changes speed.
model: The wavefronts are parallel to the boundary.
So all parts of each wavefront change speed at the same time, so there is no turning.
exam.tip: Use the wavefront idea.

exam.q: Explain, in terms of wavefronts, why light changes direction when it enters glass at an angle.
model: One side (end) of the wavefront reaches the glass first.
That part slows down.
The rest of the wavefront is still in air, travelling faster.
So the wavefront turns/pivots and changes direction, towards the normal.
exam.tip: A classic Higher 4-marker; keep to the sequence.

exam.q: Give one example of a substance that transmits one wavelength of electromagnetic radiation but absorbs another.
model: Glass (or ozone / bone and soft tissue etc.).
Transmits visible light but absorbs ultraviolet.
exam.tip: Name the substance and both wavelengths.

exam.q: Explain why a glass prism splits white light into a spectrum.
model: White light contains different wavelengths/colours.
Different wavelengths travel at different speeds in glass.
So they are refracted by different amounts (violet most, red least), separating the colours.
exam.tip: Link wavelength to speed to amount of refraction.

exam.q: Light has a frequency of 6.0 x 10^14 Hz. Its speed is 3.0 x 10^8 m/s in air and 2.0 x 10^8 m/s in glass. Calculate the change in wavelength as it enters the glass.
model: Wavelength in air = 3.0 x 10^8 / 6.0 x 10^14 = 5.0 x 10^-7 m
Wavelength in glass = 2.0 x 10^8 / 6.0 x 10^14 = 3.3 x 10^-7 m
Decrease = 1.7 x 10^-7 m
exam.tip: Same frequency in both materials.

exam.q: Describe and explain what happens to waves when they cross a boundary between two materials, and how different substances respond to different wavelengths. Use examples.
model: Waves change speed when they enter a new material.
At an angle, this causes a change in direction (refraction): slowing bends towards the normal, speeding up bends away.
Along the normal, the speed changes but the direction does not.
Frequency stays constant so wavelength changes in proportion to speed (v = f x wavelength).

Different substances absorb, transmit, refract or reflect waves differently depending on wavelength, e.g. glass transmits visible light but absorbs UV; bone absorbs X-rays but soft tissue transmits them.
Different wavelengths are refracted by different amounts, e.g. a prism disperses white light, violet most.
exam.tip: Cover both 4.10 and 4.11 with examples for top band.

worked.q: A ripple tank dipper vibrates at 4.0 Hz. In deep water the wavelength is 3.0 cm. Over a shallow plate the waves travel at 8.0 cm/s. Find the speed in deep water and the wavelength over the shallow plate, and say which way the waves bend entering the shallow region at an angle.
steps: Deep water speed: v = f x wavelength = 4.0 x 3.0 = 12 cm/s.
Frequency is unchanged over the shallow plate: f = 4.0 Hz.
Shallow wavelength = v / f = 8.0 / 4.0 = 2.0 cm.
Speed decreases (12 to 8 cm/s), so the waves bend towards the normal.
worked.ans: 12 cm/s in deep water; 2.0 cm over the plate; bend towards the normal.

worked.q: Red light of frequency 4.6 x 10^14 Hz passes from air (speed 3.0 x 10^8 m/s) into water (speed 2.25 x 10^8 m/s). Calculate its wavelength in each and state the effect on direction if it enters at an angle.
steps: Wavelength in air = v / f = 3.0 x 10^8 / 4.6 x 10^14 = 6.5 x 10^-7 m.
Frequency stays at 4.6 x 10^14 Hz in water.
Wavelength in water = 2.25 x 10^8 / 4.6 x 10^14 = 4.9 x 10^-7 m.
It slows down, so it bends towards the normal.
worked.ans: 6.5 x 10^-7 m in air, 4.9 x 10^-7 m in water; bends towards the normal.

worked.q: Explain why a swimming pool looks shallower than it really is.
steps: Light from the bottom of the pool travels up through the water to the surface.
At the surface it passes from water into air and speeds up.
Because it hits the surface at an angle, it bends away from the normal.
Your brain assumes light travels in straight lines, so it traces the rays back to a point higher than the real bottom.
worked.ans: Refraction away from the normal at the water surface makes the bottom appear raised, so the pool looks shallower.

phy_edx.3.7.summary: Sound is a **longitudinal wave** of compressions and rarefactions in the air; when it reaches a solid such as the **eardrum**, the changing pressure makes the solid **vibrate at the same frequency** as the sound. In the ear, the eardrum passes vibrations through the **ossicles** (small bones) to the fluid-filled **cochlea**, where hair cells turn them into electrical signals sent along the **auditory nerve** to the brain. These conversions only work over a **limited frequency range**, because the parts of the ear can only vibrate effectively at some frequencies, so humans hear roughly **20 Hz to 20 000 Hz (20 kHz)**.

core.h: Sound waves are vibrations of particles
core.p: Sound is a **longitudinal wave**: the particles of the medium vibrate **parallel** to the direction the wave travels. The vibrations create regions of high pressure (**compressions**) and low pressure (**rarefactions**) that move outwards from the source.
bullets: A sound source (a guitar string, a loudspeaker cone, vocal cords) vibrates and pushes on the air next to it.
The air particles pass the vibration on to neighbouring particles, but each particle only **oscillates about a fixed position**: no air travels from the source to your ear.
Sound needs a medium (solid, liquid or gas); it **cannot travel through a vacuum**.
**Frequency** of the sound = number of vibrations per second (Hz); it is heard as **pitch**.
**Amplitude** of the sound is heard as **loudness**: bigger amplitude, louder sound.

callouts.p: In a sound wave the particles vibrate parallel to the direction of energy transfer, producing compressions and rarefactions.

core.h: Converting sound waves into vibrations of a solid
core.p: When a sound wave reaches a solid surface, the **pressure on the surface keeps changing**. A compression pushes the surface **inwards**; a rarefaction (lower pressure) lets it move back **outwards**. So the solid is forced to **vibrate at the same frequency** as the sound wave. This is how sound energy is transferred into a solid such as your eardrum, a microphone diaphragm or a window pane.
bullets: Each compression gives a push, each rarefaction lets the surface move back: one in-and-out cycle per wave.
So the **frequency of vibration of the solid equals the frequency of the sound**.
A louder sound (larger amplitude) gives larger pressure changes, so the solid vibrates with a **larger amplitude**.
The vibrations then travel on through the solid as a wave (sound travels well through solids).
The reverse also happens: a vibrating solid, such as a **loudspeaker cone**, pushes on the air and creates sound waves.
A **microphone** works the first way: sound makes a diaphragm vibrate, and this is converted into an electrical signal.

callouts.p: A sound wave makes a solid vibrate at the same frequency as the sound.

core.p: The ear is a chain of energy converters. It is usually split into the **outer ear**, **middle ear** and **inner ear**. You need to know what each part does in turning sound into a signal the brain can use.
bullets: **Outer ear (pinna)**: the visible part; funnels sound waves into the ear canal.
**Ear canal**: carries the sound waves to the eardrum.
**Eardrum**: a thin, tight membrane that **vibrates** when sound waves hit it.
**Ossicles** (hammer, anvil and stirrup): three tiny bones in the middle ear that **transmit and amplify** the vibrations from the eardrum to the inner ear.
**Cochlea**: a coiled, **fluid-filled** tube in the inner ear lined with tiny **hair cells**; the vibrations make the fluid move and the hair cells move.
**Auditory nerve**: carries **electrical impulses** from the hair cells to the **brain**, which interprets them as sound.

core.h: How the ear works, step by step
core.p: This is the sequence Edexcel 6-mark questions usually want. Each step converts the disturbance from one form to another: pressure waves in air, then vibrations of a solid, then movement of fluid, then electrical signals.
bullets: 1. Sound waves (compressions and rarefactions) travel through the air and are funnelled by the pinna into the **ear canal**.
2. The changing air pressure makes the **eardrum vibrate** at the same frequency as the sound.
3. The eardrum passes the vibrations to the **ossicles**, which **amplify** them and pass them to the inner ear.
4. The vibrations make the **fluid in the cochlea** move, producing waves in the fluid.
5. Tiny **hair cells** in the cochlea move with the fluid and produce **electrical signals (impulses)**.
6. The **auditory nerve** carries these signals to the **brain**, which interprets them as sound.

callouts.p: Air wave, eardrum, ossicles, cochlea fluid, hair cells, auditory nerve, brain. Missing a link or reversing the order loses marks.

core.p: The cochlea can tell different pitches apart because **different hair cells respond to different frequencies**. The cochlea's internal membrane changes in stiffness and width along its length, so different parts vibrate most strongly at different frequencies.
bullets: High-frequency sounds make the region near the **start (base)** of the cochlea vibrate most.
Low-frequency sounds make the region near the **far end (tip)** of the cochlea vibrate most.
The brain works out pitch from **which** hair cells are sending signals.
Loudness is detected from **how strongly** the hair cells are moved (amplitude of vibration).
Hair cells damaged by very loud sounds do not regrow, which can cause permanent hearing loss at the frequencies they detected.

core.h: Why the conversion only works over a limited frequency range
core.p: A solid object such as the eardrum, the ossicles or a hair cell has **mass** and **stiffness**, so it cannot respond equally well at every frequency. Each part vibrates effectively only over a certain range of frequencies; outside that range it barely moves, so little energy is passed on and no signal is produced.
bullets: At **very high frequencies**, the parts of the ear cannot move backwards and forwards **fast enough** because of their mass (inertia), so they hardly vibrate.
At **very low frequencies**, the pressure changes are too slow for the eardrum system to pass on useful vibrations, and the hair cells do not respond.
Each structure vibrates most strongly near its own **natural frequency**; it responds well to frequencies near that and poorly to those far away.
So the **range of frequencies we can hear is limited** by the properties of the eardrum, ossicles and cochlea.
The same limit applies to microphones and loudspeakers: their diaphragms and cones only work well over certain frequency ranges.

callouts.p: Conversion of sound into vibrations only works over a limited frequency range because the solid parts can only vibrate effectively at certain frequencies.
Link the limited range to the physical properties (size, mass, stiffness) of the parts that vibrate.

core.p: A healthy young person can hear frequencies from about **20 Hz to 20 000 Hz (20 kHz)**. Sound below this range is called **infrasound** and sound above it is called **ultrasound**; these are covered in more detail in the next spec points.
bullets: **Lower limit: about 20 Hz.**
**Upper limit: about 20 kHz = 20 000 Hz.**
Below 20 Hz: **infrasound**. Above 20 kHz: **ultrasound**.
Humans are most sensitive to frequencies of a few thousand hertz (around the range of speech).
Other animals have different ranges: dogs and bats can hear ultrasound; elephants and whales communicate with infrasound.
Different ranges arise because their ears are built differently (different sizes, masses and stiffnesses of parts).

callouts.p: The range of normal human hearing is about 20 Hz to 20 kHz.
20 kHz is 20 000 Hz, not 2000 Hz. 1 kHz = 1000 Hz.
