core.p: The range of hearing is not fixed for life. The **upper limit falls with age**, and loud noise can damage the ear, reducing the range and sensitivity.
bullets: As people get older, the hair cells (especially those for high frequencies) and other parts become less responsive, so the **upper limit drops**: many adults cannot hear above about 15 kHz.
Long exposure to **loud sounds** (concerts, machinery, headphones at high volume) can damage hair cells permanently.
A damaged or perforated eardrum cannot vibrate properly, reducing hearing.
Ear defenders reduce the amplitude of sound reaching the ear by absorbing sound energy.
Hearing aids amplify sounds so that the vibrations reaching the cochlea are larger.

core.p: You can use v = f x wavelength to find the wavelengths of sounds we can hear. In air, sound travels at about 340 m/s (often 330 to 340 m/s in questions).
bullets: At 20 Hz: wavelength = 340 / 20 = **17 m**.
So audible sounds in air have wavelengths from about 1.7 cm to 17 m.
Period T = 1 / f, so a 20 kHz vibration has a period of 1 / 20 000 = 0.00005 s; the eardrum must move in and out that quickly, which shows why higher frequencies become impossible to follow.

callouts.p: Convert kHz to Hz before using v = f x wavelength.

core.p: The same conversion happens wherever sound meets a solid. Edexcel may ask about sound transmitted through walls, windows or the ground.
bullets: Sound hitting a window makes the glass vibrate, which then creates sound waves on the other side: this is how sound passes through windows and walls.
A **microphone** diaphragm is made to vibrate by sound, and the vibration is converted into a changing electrical signal.
A **loudspeaker** does the reverse: an electrical signal makes a cone vibrate, producing sound waves at the same frequency.
Heavy, massive walls vibrate less, so they transmit less sound, especially at high frequencies.
Each device has a limited frequency range over which it vibrates effectively, just like the ear.

core.p: Questions on the ear are usually explain or describe questions worth 3 to 6 marks, plus short recall of the hearing range.
bullets: Use the key words: **compressions, rarefactions, eardrum vibrates, same frequency, ossicles, cochlea, hair cells, electrical signals, auditory nerve, brain**.
Always state that the eardrum vibrates **at the same frequency as the sound**.
For the limited range, refer to the parts of the ear only vibrating effectively over a certain range of frequencies.
Quote the range as **20 Hz to 20 kHz** with units.
Do not say sound particles travel into the ear: the vibration (energy) travels, not the air.

callouts.p: Pitch depends on frequency; loudness depends on amplitude. Do not swap them.

analogy.p: Hearing is like a relay where a message is passed from runner to runner, changing form each time. The air (first runner) pushes and pulls on the eardrum, which drums the beat on to the three tiny bones, which tap a fluid-filled tube, where tiny hairs wave and send text messages (electrical signals) along a cable to the brain. The beat (frequency) stays the same all the way along. If the beat is too fast or too slow, the runners cannot keep up or cannot feel it, so the message never arrives: that is the limited hearing range. Where it breaks down: in a real relay a runner carries the baton the whole way, but in the ear no air or particles travel; only energy and the vibration pattern are passed on, and the ossicles also amplify the vibration, which a relay runner does not.

terms.d: A wave in which the particles vibrate parallel to the direction of energy transfer; sound is longitudinal.
A region in a longitudinal wave where particles are closer together, at higher pressure.
A region in a longitudinal wave where particles are further apart, at lower pressure.
The outer, visible part of the ear that funnels sound into the ear canal.
The tube that carries sound waves from the pinna to the eardrum.
A thin membrane that vibrates at the same frequency as the sound waves that hit it.
Three tiny bones in the middle ear (hammer, anvil, stirrup) that transmit and amplify vibrations from the eardrum to the cochlea.
A coiled, fluid-filled tube in the inner ear containing hair cells that convert vibrations into electrical signals.
Sensory cells in the cochlea that move with the fluid and produce electrical impulses; different cells respond to different frequencies.
The nerve that carries electrical impulses from the cochlea to the brain.
The number of vibrations per second, measured in hertz (Hz); heard as pitch.
The maximum displacement of a vibration from its rest position; heard as loudness.
How high or low a sound seems; it depends on frequency.
About 20 Hz to 20 kHz (20 000 Hz).
Sound with a frequency below 20 Hz, too low for humans to hear.
Sound with a frequency above 20 kHz, too high for humans to hear.

mistakes.w: Sound waves travel into the ear and the air particles hit the brain.
mistakes.r: The air particles only vibrate; the eardrum is made to vibrate and the signal reaches the brain as electrical impulses along the auditory nerve.

mistakes.w: The range of human hearing is 20 Hz to 2000 Hz.
mistakes.r: It is about 20 Hz to 20 kHz (20 000 Hz).

mistakes.w: The eardrum vibrates at a higher frequency to amplify the sound.
mistakes.r: The eardrum vibrates at the same frequency as the sound; the ossicles amplify the amplitude of the vibrations.

mistakes.w: The cochlea sends sound waves to the brain.
mistakes.r: Hair cells in the cochlea produce electrical signals that the auditory nerve carries to the brain.

mistakes.w: Louder sounds have a higher frequency.
mistakes.r: Louder sounds have a larger amplitude; higher pitch means higher frequency.

mistakes.w: We cannot hear ultrasound because it is too quiet.
mistakes.r: We cannot hear it because its frequency is above 20 kHz, too high for the parts of the ear to vibrate effectively.

mistakes.w: Sound can travel through space to reach astronauts.
mistakes.r: Sound needs a medium; it cannot travel through a vacuum.

mistakes.w: The hearing range gets wider with age.
mistakes.r: The upper limit of hearing decreases with age.

exam.q: State the range of frequencies a healthy human can hear.
model: About 20 Hz to 20 kHz (20 000 Hz).
exam.tip: Give both limits with units.

exam.q: Name the part of the ear that first vibrates when sound waves reach it.
model: Eardrum.
exam.tip: Not the cochlea.

exam.q: A dog whistle produces sound at 35 kHz. Explain why a human cannot hear it but a dog can.
model: 35 kHz is above the upper limit of human hearing (20 kHz), so it is ultrasound to humans.
A dog's hearing range extends to higher frequencies / its ear can vibrate at this frequency.
exam.tip: Compare the frequency with the 20 kHz limit.

exam.q: Describe how a sound wave in air makes the eardrum vibrate.
model: The sound wave consists of compressions and rarefactions (changes in pressure).
Compressions push the eardrum in; rarefactions let it move out.
So the eardrum vibrates at the same frequency as the sound wave.
exam.tip: Mention the same frequency for the last mark.

exam.q: State the function of the ossicles.
model: They transmit vibrations from the eardrum to the inner ear (cochlea).
They amplify the vibrations.
exam.tip: Two jobs: transmit and amplify.

exam.q: Calculate the wavelength of a 20 Hz sound in air. Speed of sound in air = 340 m/s.
model: wavelength = v / f = 340 / 20
exam.tip: Rearrange v = f x wavelength.

exam.q: Calculate the wavelength in air of the highest frequency a human can hear. Speed of sound = 340 m/s.
model: Highest frequency = 20 kHz = 20 000 Hz.
wavelength = 340 / 20 000
exam.tip: Convert kHz to Hz first.

exam.q: Explain why humans can only hear sounds within a limited range of frequencies.
model: Sound is converted into vibrations of solid parts of the ear (eardrum, ossicles, hair cells in the cochlea).
These parts can only vibrate effectively over a limited range of frequencies (because of their size/mass/stiffness).
At frequencies outside this range they do not vibrate enough, so no signal is sent to the brain.
exam.tip: Link the limit to the physical parts vibrating.

exam.q: Explain why an older person may not hear a high-pitched sound that a teenager can hear.
model: The upper limit of hearing decreases with age.
Because parts of the ear (hair cells) become less able to respond to high frequencies.
exam.tip: High pitch means high frequency.

exam.q: Explain how the human ear converts sound waves in the air into signals that the brain can interpret. Refer to why this process only works over a limited range of frequencies.
model: Sound waves (compressions and rarefactions) are funnelled by the pinna down the ear canal.
Pressure changes make the eardrum vibrate at the same frequency as the sound.
The ossicles transmit and amplify the vibrations to the cochlea.
Vibrations move the fluid in the cochlea, which moves hair cells; different hair cells respond to different frequencies.
Hair cells produce electrical signals carried by the auditory nerve to the brain.
The parts of the ear can only vibrate effectively over a limited range (about 20 Hz to 20 kHz), so sounds outside this range are not detected.
exam.tip: Level-marked: correct sequence plus the limited-range explanation reaches the top band.

worked.q: Speed of sound in air is 340 m/s. Find the range of wavelengths of sound that a human can hear, and the period of the highest-frequency sound.
steps: Lowest frequency 20 Hz: wavelength = v / f = 340 / 20 = 17 m.
Highest frequency 20 kHz = 20 000 Hz: wavelength = 340 / 20 000 = 0.017 m.
worked.ans: Wavelengths 0.017 m to 17 m; period of 20 kHz sound is 5 x 10^-5 s.

worked.q: A student plays notes of 50 Hz, 8 kHz and 25 kHz to a person with normal hearing. Which can the person hear, and what does the 8 kHz note do to their eardrum?
steps: Normal hearing range is 20 Hz to 20 kHz.
50 Hz is inside the range: heard.
8 kHz (8000 Hz) is inside the range: heard.
25 kHz is above 20 kHz: ultrasound, not heard.
For the 8 kHz note, the eardrum vibrates in and out 8000 times per second, the same frequency as the sound.
worked.ans: 50 Hz and 8 kHz are heard; 25 kHz is not. The eardrum vibrates at 8000 Hz for the 8 kHz note.

worked.q: Model answer: explain why sound can be heard through a closed window.
steps: Sound waves outside create compressions and rarefactions that hit the glass.
The changing pressure makes the glass vibrate at the same frequency as the sound.
The vibrating glass pushes on the air inside the room, creating new sound waves at the same frequency.
Some energy is reflected and absorbed by the glass, so the sound inside is quieter (smaller amplitude).
worked.ans: Sound is converted into vibrations of the solid glass and back into sound waves inside, at the same frequency but lower amplitude.

phy_edx.3.8.summary: Sound is classified by frequency: humans hear roughly 20 Hz to 20 000 Hz, so **ultrasound** is sound above 20 000 Hz and **infrasound** is sound below 20 Hz. Both are still mechanical, longitudinal waves, so they reflect, refract, are transmitted and are absorbed at boundaries just like audible sound. Ultrasound is used for **sonar** and **foetal scanning** because its short wavelength gives detailed echoes, while infrasound (low-frequency seismic waves) lets scientists **explore the Earth's core** and detect events such as earthquakes and volcanic eruptions.

core.p: The only thing that makes ultrasound and infrasound different from ordinary sound is their **frequency**. They are produced by vibrations, travel as longitudinal waves and need a medium, exactly like audible sound. They are simply outside the range a healthy human ear can detect.
bullets: **Ultrasound**: sound with a frequency **greater than 20 000 Hz** (20 kHz).
**Infrasound**: sound with a frequency **less than 20 Hz**.
Human hearing range: about **20 Hz to 20 000 Hz**; the upper limit falls with age.
All three are **longitudinal** waves: particles vibrate **parallel** to the direction of energy transfer, forming compressions and rarefactions.
All need a **medium** (solid, liquid or gas) and cannot travel through a vacuum.
Because v = f × λ and speed in a given medium is fixed, **higher frequency means shorter wavelength**: ultrasound has short wavelengths, infrasound long ones.

callouts.p: Sound with a frequency greater than 20 000 Hz (above the upper limit of human hearing).
Sound with a frequency less than 20 Hz (below the lower limit of human hearing).

core.h: Why the frequency matters for uses
core.p: What a wave can be used for depends on how it behaves, and that depends on its wavelength. Short-wavelength ultrasound gives sharp, detailed echoes; long-wavelength infrasound travels huge distances with little absorption.
bullets: Ultrasound's **short wavelength** means it can reflect from small objects and boundaries, giving **detailed images**.
Ultrasound can be sent as a **narrow beam** of short **pulses**, so the time of each echo can be measured precisely.
Infrasound's **long wavelength** means it is **absorbed less** and can travel very long distances through rock, water and air.
Neither can be heard by humans, so ultrasound equipment does not disturb people and infrasound must be detected with special sensors (e.g. **seismometers**).
Both obey the same wave rules: **reflection**, **refraction**, **transmission** and **absorption** at boundaries.

callouts.p: Same medium, same speed: increase frequency and wavelength must decrease. This is why ultrasound gives finer detail than audible sound.

core.p: Every ultrasound use relies on the same idea. A pulse of ultrasound is sent out. When it reaches a **boundary between two different media**, some of the wave is **reflected** back as an echo and the rest is **transmitted** onward. A detector records **when** the echo returns and how **strong** it is.
bullets: Ultrasound is **partially reflected** at each boundary between materials of different density.
The **time** between sending the pulse and receiving the echo tells you **how far away** the boundary is.
Distance to the boundary = (speed × time) ÷ 2, because the pulse travels **there and back**.
The **strength** of the echo gives information about the type of boundary.
Echoes from many boundaries at different depths are combined by a computer to **build up an image**.
The same device usually acts as both **transmitter** and **receiver** (a transducer).

callouts.p: The echo time is for the round trip. Forgetting to divide by 2 doubles your distance and loses the final mark.

core.p: Sonar (sound navigation and ranging) is used by ships and submarines to find the **depth of the sea**, locate **shoals of fish**, find **wrecks** and detect **submarines**. A transmitter on the hull sends a pulse of ultrasound down through the water; the pulse reflects off the seabed or an object and the echo is detected by a receiver.
bullets: Pulse of **ultrasound** sent from the ship into the water.
Pulse **reflects** off the seabed (or a fish shoal) and returns as an **echo**.
The **time** for the pulse to return is measured.
Depth = (speed of sound in water × time) ÷ 2; speed of sound in sea water is about **1500 m/s**.
A shorter echo time means a **shallower** sea or a **closer** object.
Ultrasound is used because its short wavelength gives **accurate** detection of small objects, and its narrow beam can be **directed**.
Bats and dolphins use the same principle (**echolocation**) to find food and navigate.

callouts.p: In explain questions say clearly: pulse sent, reflects off seabed, echo detected, time measured, distance = speed × time ÷ 2.

core.p: Ultrasound is used to produce images of a **foetus** (unborn baby) in the womb. A probe is placed on the mother's abdomen with a **gel** between them. Pulses of ultrasound enter the body and are **partially reflected** at each **boundary between different tissues** (for example between amniotic fluid and the foetus's skin, or between soft tissue and bone).
bullets: The probe sends **pulses** of ultrasound into the body and detects the **echoes**.
At each tissue boundary, **some** ultrasound is **reflected** and the rest is **transmitted** deeper.
The **time** taken for each echo gives the **depth** of each boundary.
The **strength** (amplitude) of each echo depends on the materials either side of the boundary.
A computer uses the timings and strengths to build up an **image** on a screen.
The **gel** removes air between probe and skin; without it most ultrasound would be reflected at the skin and little would enter the body.
It is **safe** for the foetus and mother because ultrasound is **not ionising**, unlike X-rays, which could damage the developing cells.
It is **non-invasive** (no surgery) and gives a **real-time** moving image.

callouts.p: X-rays are ionising and can damage cells and DNA in a rapidly developing foetus. Ultrasound is non-ionising, so it is used instead.

core.p: The same echo principle is used beyond medicine and sonar. You may meet these as unfamiliar contexts in the exam; apply the same pulse, echo, time and partial-reflection reasoning.
bullets: **Detecting flaws** (cracks) in metal castings, pipes, welds and rails: an unexpected echo arrives **earlier** than the echo from the far side, showing a crack.
**Medical imaging** of organs such as the heart, kidneys and liver.
**Echolocation** by bats and dolphins to locate prey and obstacles.
**Cleaning** delicate objects such as jewellery (vibrations shake dirt loose).
**Breaking up kidney stones** with high-energy ultrasound, avoiding surgery.

callouts.p: Edexcel often gives a new use. Always mention: ultrasound pulse, reflection at a boundary, time of echo, and distance = speed × time ÷ 2.

core.h: Use 3: Exploring the Earth's core with seismic waves
core.p: Earthquakes produce **seismic waves** that travel through the Earth. Much of their energy is at very low frequencies, in the **infrasound** range. Scientists use **seismometers** at many places on the surface to record when and where the waves arrive. Because nobody can drill to the core, these waves are our main evidence for the Earth's internal structure.
bullets: **P-waves** (primary) are **longitudinal** and can travel through **solids and liquids**; they are faster.
**S-waves** (secondary) are **transverse** and can travel through **solids only**, not liquids.
Seismic waves **refract** (change speed and direction) as density changes with depth, so their paths **curve**.
S-waves are **not detected** on the opposite side of the Earth from the earthquake: there is a large **S-wave shadow zone**.
This shows the **outer core is liquid**, because S-waves cannot pass through liquids.
P-waves **refract** sharply at the mantle/core boundary, producing a **P-wave shadow zone** where few or no P-waves arrive.
The sizes of the shadow zones let scientists work out the **size of the core**.
Faint P-waves detected inside the P-wave shadow zone give evidence that the **inner core is solid**.

callouts.p: S-waves cannot travel through liquids and are not detected on the far side of the Earth, so the outer core must be liquid.

core.p: Infrasound travels a long way with little energy absorbed, so it is useful for **long-range detection** of very large events, and some animals use it to communicate over many kilometres.
bullets: Detecting and monitoring **earthquakes** using seismometers.
Detecting **volcanic eruptions**, which give out infrasound before and during eruption.
Detecting **meteors** entering the atmosphere and large **explosions**, including nuclear test monitoring.
**Animal communication**: elephants and some whales produce and detect infrasound over long distances.
Tracking the movement of animals in remote areas by their infrasound calls.

callouts.p: Its long wavelength means less energy is absorbed by the medium per kilometre, so it can be detected far from the source.

core.p: Exam questions often ask you to compare the two or to choose which is suitable for a job. Base the choice on wavelength, detail and range.
bullets: Ultrasound: **high frequency**, **short wavelength**, good **detail**, absorbed more so **shorter range**.
Infrasound: **low frequency**, **long wavelength**, little detail, absorbed less so **long range**.
Both are **longitudinal** mechanical waves; both cannot pass through a **vacuum**.
Both are **inaudible** to humans.

core.p: Six-mark questions reward a logical chain. For any echo use, follow the sequence below; for the Earth's core, link the wave property to the observation and then to the conclusion.
bullets: Echo chain: **pulse sent** → travels through medium → **partially reflected at boundary** → **echo detected** → **time measured** → distance = speed × time ÷ 2 → many echoes build **image**.

Earth chain: earthquake produces **P and S waves** → detected by **seismometers** around the world → S-waves **not detected** on far side → S-waves **cannot travel through liquid** → **outer core is liquid**.
Add **refraction**: changing density changes wave speed, so paths **curve** and P-waves bend at the core boundary.
Finish with a **safety or advantage** point where relevant (non-ionising, non-invasive, long range).

callouts.p: Edexcel 6-mark answers are marked by levels. Use the technical words: pulse, reflect, boundary, echo, time, speed, transmitted, refracted, longitudinal, transverse.

analogy.p: Sonar and foetal scanning are like shouting into a canyon and timing the echo: the longer the wait, the further the cliff, and you halve the time because the sound went there and back. Using ultrasound is like shouting with a very high, sharp click rather than a low rumble, so even small ledges send back a clear echo. The analogy breaks down because in the body and sea the wave is only partially reflected at each boundary and carries on to make more echoes, whereas a canyon wall reflects almost everything; also ultrasound and infrasound are inaudible, so detectors, not ears, pick up the echoes.

The number of waves passing a point each second, measured in hertz (Hz).
The distance from one point on a wave to the same point on the next wave, e.g. compression to compression.
A wave in which the particles vibrate parallel to the direction of energy transfer.
A reflected sound wave detected after it returns from a boundary.
A short burst of waves, sent so that the time of its echo can be measured.
Using pulses of ultrasound and the timing of their echoes to find the depth of water or the position of objects underwater.
When only some of a wave is reflected at a boundary and the rest is transmitted into the next material.
Using ultrasound echoes from tissue boundaries to build an image of an unborn baby.
Waves produced by earthquakes that travel through the Earth; much of their energy is infrasound.
A longitudinal seismic wave that can travel through solids and liquids.
A transverse seismic wave that can travel through solids but not liquids.
A region of the Earth's surface where particular seismic waves from an earthquake are not detected.
An instrument that detects and records seismic waves.
Does not have enough energy to remove electrons from atoms, so does not damage cells or DNA in this way.

exam.q: State what is meant by ultrasound.
model: Sound with a frequency above 20 000 Hz (above the range of human hearing).
exam.tip: Give the number with units: 20 000 Hz or 20 kHz.

exam.q: State the frequency range of infrasound.
model: Below 20 Hz.
exam.tip: Do not confuse with the lower limit of hearing; infrasound is less than this.

exam.q: Which of these frequencies is ultrasound? A 15 Hz  B 2 kHz  C 18 kHz  D 45 kHz
model: D (45 kHz = 45 000 Hz, which is greater than 20 000 Hz).
exam.tip: Convert kHz to Hz first.

exam.q: A ship sends a pulse of ultrasound to the seabed. The echo is received 0.60 s later. The speed of sound in sea water is 1500 m/s. Calculate the depth of the sea.
model: distance travelled = 1500 × 0.60 = 900 m
this is there and back, so divide by 2
depth = 450 m
exam.tip: Write the equation, substitute, then halve.

exam.q: Explain why gel is placed between the ultrasound probe and the skin during a foetal scan.
model: Removes air between probe and skin
so less ultrasound is reflected at the skin and more is transmitted into the body
exam.tip: Link to reflection at a boundary.

exam.q: Give two reasons why ultrasound, rather than X-rays, is used to scan a foetus.
model: Ultrasound is non-ionising / does not damage cells or DNA (X-rays are ionising)
Ultrasound can show soft tissue / gives a real-time image / is non-invasive
exam.tip: The ionising point is the one examiners most expect.

exam.q: Explain how ultrasound is used to produce an image of a foetus.
model: Probe sends pulses of ultrasound into the body
Ultrasound is partially reflected at boundaries between different tissues
Echoes are detected and the time for each echo is measured to give the depth of each boundary
A computer uses the timings (and strengths) of the echoes to build up an image
exam.tip: Use the word boundary and mention time measurement.

exam.q: Explain why ultrasound is suitable for detecting a crack inside a metal rail.
model: Ultrasound is reflected at the crack (a boundary between metal and air)
the echo returns earlier than the echo from the far side of the rail, showing the crack's position
exam.tip: Compare echo times.

exam.q: Explain why elephants are able to communicate with each other over distances of several kilometres using infrasound.
model: Infrasound has a long wavelength / low frequency
so it is absorbed less and travels long distances
exam.tip: Link low frequency to low absorption.

exam.q: Seismic waves from an earthquake are recorded at stations all around the world. Explain how these observations provide evidence for the structure of the Earth's core.
model: Earthquakes produce P-waves and S-waves (infrasound), detected by seismometers
P-waves are longitudinal and can travel through solids and liquids
S-waves are transverse and can only travel through solids
S-waves are not detected on the opposite side of the Earth: an S-wave shadow zone
so the outer core must be liquid
waves refract as density changes, so paths curve; P-waves refract at the core boundary giving a P-wave shadow zone
size of the shadow zones gives the size of the core; P-waves in the shadow zone suggest a solid inner core
exam.tip: Structure: wave properties, observation, conclusion. Level 3 needs a linked chain.

exam.q: Explain why ultrasound produces more detailed images than audible sound.
model: Ultrasound has a higher frequency so a shorter wavelength (v = f λ)
so it reflects from smaller objects/boundaries, giving more detail
exam.tip: Mention v = f λ to justify shorter wavelength.

worked.q: A fishing boat's sonar detects an echo from a shoal of fish 0.08 s after the pulse is sent. The speed of sound in sea water is 1500 m/s. How deep is the shoal?
steps: Equation: distance = speed × time
Total distance = 1500 m/s × 0.08 s = 120 m
This is the distance there and back, so depth = 120 ÷ 2 = 60 m
worked.ans: The shoal is 60 m below the boat.

worked.q: An ultrasound scanner sends a pulse into the body. An echo from the boundary of an organ returns after 0.000 13 s. Ultrasound travels at 1540 m/s in soft tissue. Calculate the depth of the boundary.
steps: distance = speed × time = 1540 × 0.000 13 = 0.2002 m
Divide by 2 for the round trip: 0.2002 ÷ 2 = 0.1001 m
Convert: 0.100 m = about 10 cm
worked.ans: The boundary is about 0.10 m (10 cm) below the skin.

worked.q: Model answer: Explain why no S-waves are detected on the opposite side of the Earth from an earthquake.
steps: S-waves are transverse waves.
Transverse seismic waves cannot travel through liquids.
The S-waves reach the outer core and cannot pass through it.
Therefore the outer core must be liquid, creating an S-wave shadow zone on the far side.
worked.ans: S-waves cannot travel through liquid, so they are stopped by the liquid outer core, leaving a shadow zone opposite the earthquake.

phy_edx.3.9.summary: When a sound wave passes from one medium into another, its **frequency stays the same** because it is set by the source, but its **speed changes** because the new medium transmits vibrations at a different rate. Since v = f × λ and f is fixed, the **wavelength changes in proportion to the speed**: faster medium, longer wavelength; slower medium, shorter wavelength. Sound is generally fastest in solids, slower in liquids and slowest in gases, and if it meets the boundary at an angle the change of speed also makes it **refract** (change direction).

core.p: This spec point is about how three quantities are **inter-related** when sound crosses a boundary between two media, such as air to water or air to a brick wall. One quantity never changes, and the other two change together.
bullets: **Frequency**: does **not change**. It is fixed by the vibrating **source**.
**Speed (velocity)**: **changes**, because it depends on the **medium** the wave is in.
**Wavelength**: **changes**, in the **same proportion** as the speed.
Linking equation: **v = f × λ** (wave speed = frequency × wavelength).
If speed increases, wavelength increases; if speed decreases, wavelength decreases.
Speed ÷ wavelength = frequency stays constant on both sides of the boundary.

head: Quantity
Changes at boundary?
Why
rows: set by the source; waves per second cannot change
λ = v ÷ f, so λ follows v

callouts.p: When sound passes into a different medium, the frequency stays the same, the speed changes and therefore the wavelength changes (v = f × λ).

core.p: Think of the boundary as a line that wavefronts arrive at. Each compression that reaches the boundary from one side makes one compression set off on the other side. So the number of waves arriving per second must equal the number leaving per second. If it did not, waves would have to pile up at the boundary or appear from nowhere, which cannot happen.
bullets: Frequency = **number of waves passing a point per second**.
Each wave arriving at the boundary produces **one** wave in the new medium.
So waves per second on both sides are **equal**: frequency is **unchanged**.
Frequency is decided by the **source** (how fast it vibrates), not by the medium.
This is why the **pitch** of a sound is the same when you hear it through water or through a wall (pitch depends on frequency).

callouts.p: Students often say frequency increases when sound speeds up. It does not: the wavelength stretches instead.

core.p: Sound is a **longitudinal** wave that travels by particles vibrating and passing the vibration on to their neighbours. How quickly that happens depends on how the particles are arranged and bonded in the medium.
bullets: In **solids**, particles are **close together** and **strongly bonded**, so vibrations pass on **quickly**: sound is **fastest**.
In **liquids**, particles are close but less strongly held: sound is **slower than in solids**.
In **gases**, particles are **far apart**, so vibrations pass on **slowly**: sound is **slowest**.
Typical speeds: air about **330 to 340 m/s**, water about **1500 m/s**, steel about **5000 to 6000 m/s**.
Sound cannot travel through a **vacuum** because there are no particles to vibrate.
In a gas, sound travels faster when the gas is **warmer**, because the particles move faster.

core.p: Rearranging the wave equation gives **λ = v ÷ f**. Because f is fixed at the boundary, λ is **directly proportional** to v. Whatever factor the speed changes by, the wavelength changes by the same factor.
bullets: Air to water: speed goes from about 330 m/s to 1500 m/s (about **4.5 times faster**), so wavelength becomes about **4.5 times longer**.
Water to air: speed **decreases**, so wavelength becomes **shorter**.
Air to steel: speed increases a lot, so wavelength becomes **much longer**.
Compressions are **spaced further apart** in the faster medium, because each one travels further before the next one is made.
The **amplitude** usually decreases after the boundary because some energy is **reflected** and some is **absorbed**, but this is separate from the f, v, λ relationship.

callouts.p: λ2 ÷ λ1 = v2 ÷ v1. If the speed doubles, the wavelength doubles; if the speed halves, the wavelength halves.

core.h: Putting it together with v = f × λ
core.p: Every calculation on this point uses the same two steps. First use the medium you know everything about to find the frequency, then use that same frequency in the new medium.
bullets: Step 1: find **f** in the first medium: f = v1 ÷ λ1.
Step 2: **same f** in the second medium.
Step 3: find the new wavelength **λ2 = v2 ÷ f** (or the new speed v2 = f × λ2).
Units: v in **m/s**, f in **Hz**, λ in **m**.
Check your answer: faster medium must give a **longer** wavelength.

callouts.p: wave speed (m/s) = frequency (Hz) × wavelength (m); v = f × λ

core.p: If the sound meets the boundary **at an angle** to the normal, one side of each wavefront enters the new medium and changes speed before the other side. This makes the wave **change direction**: this is **refraction**. If the wave travels **along the normal** (at 90 degrees to the boundary), it changes speed and wavelength but **not direction**.
bullets: Refraction happens because of the **change in speed** at the boundary.
Entering a medium where sound is **faster** (e.g. air to water): the sound bends **away from the normal**.
Entering a medium where sound is **slower** (e.g. water to air): the sound bends **towards the normal**.
Note this is the **opposite** of light: light slows down in water and glass, but sound speeds up.
Frequency is still unchanged during refraction; only speed, wavelength and direction change.

callouts.p: Light bends towards the normal going into water because it slows down. Sound bends away from the normal going into water because it speeds up.

core.h: Worked direction: gas to liquid to solid
core.p: A common exam setting is a sound made in air that then travels into water or into a solid (for example a train on a rail, or a whale call heard by a diver). Use the order of speeds to predict the changes.
bullets: Air to water: **f same, v increases, λ increases**.
Water to air: **f same, v decreases, λ decreases**.
Air to steel rail: **f same, v increases greatly, λ increases greatly**.
Sound through a rail arrives **before** sound through the air because it travels faster in the solid.
Going between two gases at different temperatures (warm to cold air): speed decreases, so λ decreases, f same.

core.p: Our ears detect **frequency** as **pitch**. Because the frequency of a sound does not change as it passes from one medium to another, a note keeps the same pitch whether it reaches you through air, water or a wall.
bullets: Pitch depends on **frequency**, not wavelength or speed.
A note under water has a **longer wavelength** but the **same pitch** as in air.
Loudness depends on **amplitude**, which usually falls at a boundary because energy is reflected and absorbed.

callouts.p: Same frequency means same pitch, even though the wavelength has changed.

core.h: What happens to energy at the boundary
core.p: At a boundary, a sound wave can be **reflected**, **transmitted** or **absorbed**, often all three. Only the **transmitted** part continues into the new medium with the new speed and wavelength.
bullets: **Reflected** part stays in the first medium with the **original** speed and wavelength (an echo).
**Transmitted** part enters the new medium: **same frequency**, new speed, new wavelength.
**Absorbed** energy increases the internal (thermal) energy store of the material.
Because energy is split, the transmitted sound is usually **quieter** (smaller amplitude).

core.h: Exam technique for describe and explain questions
core.p: This point is often tested with a 2 to 4 mark describe question or as part of a 6 mark question. State all three quantities and give the reason.
bullets: Always state the **frequency** change explicitly: **stays the same**.
State the **direction** of the speed change (increases or decreases) with a reason based on the medium.
State the wavelength change and link it with **v = f × λ**.
For calculations, show f first, then the new λ or v, with units.
Use the word **medium** (plural **media**), not material, where possible.

callouts.p: Frequency: same (set by source). Speed: changes (depends on medium). Wavelength: changes in proportion to speed because v = f × λ.

analogy.t: Marching band crossing from road to mud
analogy.p: Imagine a marching band stepping in time to a drum. When the band walks from a road onto a faster moving walkway, the drummer still beats at the same rate, so the number of steps per second (frequency) is unchanged. But each step now carries the marchers further, so the gap between rows (wavelength) grows. Walking back onto the road, they slow and the rows bunch up. If the band crosses the edge at an angle, one end of each row speeds up first and the whole line swings round, which is refraction. The analogy breaks down because in a real sound wave no particles travel across the boundary: only the vibration (energy) is passed on, and some of it is reflected back rather than all crossing over.

terms.d: The substance (solid, liquid or gas) a wave travels through; plural media.
The surface where two different media meet.
The number of waves passing a point each second, measured in hertz (Hz); set by the source.
The distance from one point on a wave to the same point on the next wave, e.g. compression to compression, measured in metres.
The distance a wave (its energy) travels per second, measured in m/s; depends on the medium.
v = f × λ: wave speed = frequency × wavelength.
A wave in which the particles vibrate parallel to the direction of energy transfer; sound is longitudinal.
A region of a longitudinal wave where the particles are closer together.
A region of a longitudinal wave where the particles are further apart.
The change in direction of a wave when it crosses a boundary at an angle, caused by a change in speed.
An imaginary line at 90 degrees to a boundary at the point where the wave meets it.
When a wave passes through a boundary into the next medium.
How high or low a sound seems; determined by its frequency.
Two quantities that change by the same factor; at a fixed frequency, wavelength is directly proportional to speed.

mistakes.w: When sound goes into water its frequency increases.
mistakes.r: Frequency stays the same; it is set by the source.

mistakes.w: Sound travels faster in air than in water because air is less dense.
mistakes.r: Sound travels faster in water (about 1500 m/s) than in air (about 330 m/s); it is fastest in solids.

mistakes.w: When sound speeds up the wavelength gets shorter.
mistakes.r: At constant frequency, wavelength is proportional to speed (v = f × λ), so faster means a longer wavelength.

mistakes.w: Sound bends towards the normal when entering water, like light.
mistakes.r: Sound speeds up in water, so it bends away from the normal.

mistakes.w: The wave always changes direction at a boundary.
mistakes.r: It only changes direction if it meets the boundary at an angle; along the normal it changes speed and wavelength only.

mistakes.w: The pitch changes when sound goes into water.
mistakes.r: Pitch depends on frequency, which does not change, so pitch stays the same.

mistakes.w: Particles of air travel into the water carrying the sound.
mistakes.r: The particles only vibrate about fixed positions; energy is transferred across the boundary, not particles.

mistakes.w: Speed changes because the frequency changes.
mistakes.r: Speed changes because the medium changes; frequency stays constant and wavelength changes instead.

exam.q: A sound wave travels from air into water. State what happens to the frequency of the wave.
model: It stays the same / does not change.
exam.tip: One word answers like 'same' are fine for 1 mark.

exam.q: State what happens to the speed of a sound wave as it passes from air into a steel rail.
model: It increases.
exam.tip: Sound is fastest in solids.

exam.q: Describe how the speed, frequency and wavelength of a sound wave change as it passes from air into water.
model: Frequency stays the same
Speed increases
Wavelength increases
exam.tip: Give all three quantities separately.

exam.q: Explain why the wavelength of a sound wave increases when it travels from air into water.
model: Frequency is unchanged (and speed increases)
since v = f × λ, wavelength must increase in proportion
exam.tip: Quote the equation in words or symbols.

exam.q: Explain why the frequency of a sound wave does not change when it enters a new medium.
model: Frequency is determined by the source
the number of waves arriving at the boundary each second equals the number leaving
exam.tip: Mention the source.

exam.q: A sound of frequency 500 Hz travels in air at 340 m/s. Calculate its wavelength in air.
exam.tip: Rearrange before substituting.

exam.q: The 500 Hz sound then enters water, where the speed of sound is 1500 m/s. Calculate its wavelength in water.
model: frequency stays 500 Hz
exam.tip: State that f is unchanged to earn the first mark.

exam.q: A sound wave has a wavelength of 0.20 m in air (speed 330 m/s). In a block of material the same sound has a wavelength of 1.2 m. Calculate the speed of sound in the material.
model: frequency is the same in the material
exam.tip: Find f first, then reuse it.

exam.q: Explain why sound travels faster in solids than in gases.
model: In solids particles are closer together / strongly bonded
so vibrations are passed from particle to particle more quickly
exam.tip: Refer to particles and passing on vibrations.

exam.q: A diver underwater hears a boat engine. Sound from the engine travels through air and then into water at an angle to the surface. Explain the changes that happen to the sound wave as it crosses the surface.
model: Sound is a longitudinal wave transferring energy by vibrating particles
frequency stays the same because it is set by the source
speed increases because sound travels faster in water (liquid) than air (gas)
wavelength increases because v = f × λ with f constant
the wave meets the boundary at an angle so it refracts
it bends away from the normal because it speeds up
some sound is reflected and some absorbed, so amplitude/loudness of transmitted sound decreases; pitch unchanged
exam.tip: Cover f, v, λ, direction and energy for a full level 3 answer.

worked.q: A whistle produces sound of frequency 2000 Hz. The speed of sound in air is 340 m/s and in water is 1500 m/s. Calculate the wavelength in air and in water, and state the factor by which the wavelength changes.
steps: Frequency stays 2000 Hz in water
worked.ans: 0.17 m in air, 0.75 m in water: the wavelength is about 4.4 times longer in water, the same factor as the speed increase.

worked.q: Sound travels along a steel rail where its wavelength is 2.5 m and its speed is 5000 m/s. It then passes into the air, where the speed is 330 m/s. Calculate its frequency and its wavelength in air.
steps: Frequency is unchanged when the sound enters the air: 2000 Hz
Check: slower medium gives shorter wavelength, as expected
worked.ans: Frequency 2000 Hz; wavelength in air 0.165 m (about 0.17 m).

worked.q: Model answer: A sound passes straight down (along the normal) from water into air. Describe what happens to its speed, frequency, wavelength and direction.
steps: Frequency: stays the same, because it is set by the source.
Speed: decreases, because sound travels more slowly in a gas than in a liquid.
Wavelength: decreases, because v = f × λ and f is constant.
Direction: does not change, because it travels along the normal.
worked.ans: Same frequency, lower speed, shorter wavelength, no change in direction.
